answer: Four objects form the chain. pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> turns supervision on for that port and bin: set tca-supervision true and data-supervision true; show also lists supported-parameters (max 100 elements). pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> carries the limits for that instance: add or set with low-threshold and high-threshold, values are Number (uint64, int64, decimal64), na or not-supported, default na. pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> holds the per-type values and shows default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, for example set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200. pm-resource-<resource> gates real-time-supervision (default true) and show pm displays the counters. direction defaults to all, location defaults to all.

Create the key first: add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <sha-1|aes-cmac|sha-256|md5> key-value <string 8..40> is-trusted true. key-id range is 1..65534 and is-trusted defaults to false. Then add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>, where ip-address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS name; origin is dhcp or manual (default manual), admin-state defaults to unlock, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. Enable globally with set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true; ntp-enabled defaults to true, ntp-auth-enabled defaults to false, assignment-method is manual, dhcp or both (default both). To check it works: show ntp ntp-active-server, then show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means every recent probe was answered), stratum, offset, jitter, delay, poll and condition. show clock time-source reads ntp once synchronised.

They address different things. protection-switch moves traffic on a protection group: protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>, with operation-type force, lockout, manual or release. switch-target is not needed for release and lockout. Example: protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection. manual-switchover moves the controller: manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<AID>, for example manual-switchover card-1-3 on a G42, card-1-5 on a G32, card-1-12 on a G34c. It prompts that the controller will switch over and the connection to the management interface will be lost, so confirm at the prompt or use -f. Both are Operational mode only. Check show controller-card redundancy-status and redundancy-standby-status before switching a controller.

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an active NTP source is what rejects it. Run show clock: time-source is ntp or manual (default manual), and it also gives current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, DST-active and last-time-jump in the form <time1> to <time2> (jumps under 10 seconds are ignored). Check show ntp for ntp-enabled and ntp-active-server, and show ntp-server-status-<ip-address> for reach, stratum, offset and auth-status. If you must set it by hand, first set ntp ntp-enabled false, then set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z, ISO 8601 derived format with Z for UTC or +/-hh:mm for another zone. The time command shows the system time in the configured timezone, not the one used in set-time.

show ne gives the identity: ne-id, ne-name (default 1830 GX), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-site, ne-location, clli, contact, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), plus recover-mode, recover-mode-reason, equipment-discovery-ready and alarm-report-ready. For contents, show chassis, show slot (supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state, current-equipment), show card-<name> and show inventory (actual-type, serial-number, clei, part-number, PON, hardware-version, fw-status). The cost is in restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]: type warm is the default and is non service affecting, with connectivity back within five minutes; cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. With no resource-id the active controller card is restarted. show card resources lists sub-components.

Slot 2 of chassis 1 is slot-1-2: show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> gives AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The card in it is card-1-2, created with add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>, optionally subslot-name for sub-cards (subslot-name can only be set at creation). Under the card hang port objects, port-<card-name>-<port-name>, which are system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. In a pluggable cage you add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <CFP2-DCO|OSFP|QSFP28|QSFPDD|QSFPDD-ZR|QSFPPLUS|SFP|SFPPLUS>; the tributary port termination point is auto-created with the TOM and auto-deleted with it. The pluggable FRU data is show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>, for example show inventory-1-3-1, giving actual-type, actual-subtype, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code and fw-status.

Capability lives in the supported-* objects, keyed by card-type rather than by the installed instance. show supported-card-<card-type> gives supported-subtype, supported-card-mode and default-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, category (controller, line-card, fan, power-supply, other, carrier-card, blank), max-power-draw, is-field-replaceable, console-port-support and supported-bands. show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> gives port-type, direction, default-tom and allows-auto-migration; show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> gives supported-subtype, supported-phy-modes and default-phy-mode; show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> gives possible-card-types. What the fitted unit is doing is show card-<name>: required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, power-profile, category, last-reboot-reason, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state.

The parents must exist first. add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad>, instance-id 0..255, version ospfv2 (default) or ospfv3, router-id-mode manual or use-loopback (default use-loopback, which requires an ipv4 LO-MGMT address). Then add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>; the OSPF instance must be created before the area, ospf-area-type is normal. Then add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>; instance and area must both be present. Its defaults are enable true, hello-interval 10 s (1..32767), router-dead-interval 40 s (4..65535), ospf-cost 10, priority 1, ospf-if-routing auto. Progress is in show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id>: state moves down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, with role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. The neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down, and both NEs need instance, area and interface with the DCN bridges connected.

Per card use show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>, where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, for example show software-load-1-5/active. It reports swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-pkg-type. The individual pieces are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> with state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version and description, and below them show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>, for example show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb. The bundled firmware is show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> with fw-version; compare it with show current-fw, which gives fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status.

The per-port switch is lldp-admin-status, present on comm-eth-<card-name>-<port-name> and on ethernet: tx-only, rx-only, tx-and-rx or disabled, default disabled, for example set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. On ethernet there are also lldp-ingress-mode and lldp-egress-mode (disabled, snoop, drop, snoop-and-drop, default disabled). show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> shows what the node sends: chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, system-name the NE name. show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress gives the counts: total-frames-out proves transmission, total-frames-in reception, plus total-discarded-frames, error-frames, total-discarded-tlvs and total-ageouts, all defaulting to 0. Egress direction is not supported and all counters freeze while lldp-admin-status is disabled. Peers appear in show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress; the global show lldp hold-on-timer defaults to 900 seconds.

show slot lists every position as slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> with AID, supported-type, installed-type (blank when nothing is fitted), oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> gives the FRU record of whatever is installed: actual-type, actual-subtype, hardware-version, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes and fw-status, which is not-applicable, current, not-current or unavailable (default not-applicable). The running level per firmware image is show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name> with fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable; default unavailable), for example current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 against expected 0x28 shows not-current.

show manifest lists the downloaded manifest files, and show manifest-<manifest-file> gives manifest-signature, downloaded-on (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and information. The contents are show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name>, giving state, version and description; state is where you see whether each piece got installed, with values installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown). show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> gives the bundled fw-version, and show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type> gives the packaged FRU information for an equipment-type. Once the package is a software load on a card, the equivalent views are show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> and show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>, with the same installed / not-installed / installation-failed / unknown states.

Both come from per resource-type profiles. Alarm severity: set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>, with direction na, ingress or egress and location na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value> edits the same profile, which is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. PM: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision <true|false> default-tca-supervision <true|false> decides what newly created resources of that type get. Globally, set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled or manual (default manual, meaning supervision is controlled per pm-profile-entry or per pm-control-entry). Default threshold values live in pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/... as default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold.

ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> makes that decision: action is protect, bypass or discard, default protect. It also carries the mandatory priority (uint8, used to give precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel or transport (default tunnel), esn (default true), anti-replay-window 32..1024 (default 64, only when action is protect) and dynamic-ts (default disabled). Underneath hangs ipsec-traffic-selector-<local-instance>/<peer>/<spd-entry>/<ts-name> with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0..255; default any), and under each selector local-subnet and remote-subnet keyed .../<prefix>, and local-ports and remote-ports keyed .../<start>/<stop>. The SPD entries for a peer are grouped by security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>, whose associated-secure-entity lists them.

trusted-certificate-<id> is the CA you trust: the X509v3 CA root and intermediate certificates trusted by the system. local-certificate-<id> is this node's own identity, the end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities; its used-by attribute lists the secure-applications and ikev2-peers presently using it, and trust-chain lists the trusted certificates above it. peer-certificate-<id> is the far end: the trusted remote peer end-entity certificate for the L1 encryption secure application, and it uniquely carries white-listed, which is true when it was imported with no trust chain. The fourth name, certificate, is not a per-certificate object: show certificates lists all managed local, trusted and peer certificates, show certificate-revocation lists revocations, and clear certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id> removes one.

It goes on with import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>], Operational mode only, where certificate type is trusted-certificate, local-certificate or peer-certificate. Example: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>. The -i flag also imports intermediate certificates present in a PEM bundle, or those referenced by the AIA extension; root certificates must be installed individually, and with no certificate-name the name is derived from the topmost issuer CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1. Certificates can also arrive by the download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles. To take one off: clear [-f] certificate type=<trusted|local|peer> id=<id>, and the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate. Bulk types are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. display-cert shows the details.

access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name> is the one that permits or denies: action permit or deny is mandatory when the rule is created, and the match is narrowed by module-name (default *), path (XPath of a data node, notification, RPC or an external command; default *), attribute and attribute-value (leaf-lists, max 10 entries of up to 64 chars) and operation (bits create, read, update, delete, execute; default * for all). access-rule-list-<name> is the grouping and ordering object: the list is processed in order given by sequence-id, and user-group names which user-groups it applies to (default *, all). sw-control-rule-<service-name> has nothing to do with traffic: it overrides what happens when a software service fails, with fail-action default-action, ignore or system-restart. access-control-list is read-only, show access-control-list. Packet filtering proper is acl and ace.

Ordering is by sequence-id and lower number ids are processed first, so the rule with the lower sequence-id takes effect. sequence-id is a uint16, applied both to each access-rule within its list and to the access-rule-list itself; if you do not provide one it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the entry goes to the end of the list. The id can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On access-rule-list-<name>, user-group is a leaf-list of user-group names or the match-all default *, and a maximum of 20 user-groups can be referenced. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists. Both commands run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trap community string is not in snmp-community; the guide states the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it with add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> trap-community-string <value>, or set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>. It is a string of 0..32 characters and defaults to infinera, which is what a receiver rejects if it was never changed. The rest of the target: snmp-version v2c (default) or v3, snmpv3-user only when the version is v3, target-address as IPv4/IPv6 or hostname, target-port 0..65535 default 162, target-transport udp, enabled default true. snmp-community-<name> holds only read access strings: community-string 1..32 chars, community-string-access read-only, enabled default true. Global control is set snmp enabled <true|false> and port (1..65535, default 161).

external-fiber-connection is the one written by something other than you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it can be configured manually that is not recommended. It represents a physical link between ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or within one NE in disaggregated configurations, addressed as external-fiber-connection-<name> with src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way) and scope general-purpose or cable-id (default general-purpose; cable-id is required for CableID path verification). fiber-connection-<name> is the user-provisioned link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE, with src-port, dst-port and fiber-connection-type. supporting-fiber-connection-<name> is show only, returning the fiber-connection-list for an entity.

For the node's own address use ipv4-address: add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>, for example add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0 or add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'. show returns netmask and origin (static, dhcp, auto-config; default static). The other two are read-only LLDP views, not configuration. management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address advertised by the remote system seen on that port, with if-subtype, if-id and address-oid. management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address> reports the management address this node advertises in its own LLDP, with if-subtype unknown, if-index or system-port-number. Neither assigns an address to an interface.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Check show interface-<if-name>: ipv4-address-assignment-method is static or dhcp (default static) and ipv4-enabled is true or false (default true); use set interface-<if-name> ipv4-address-assignment-method static before retrying. The address is validated too: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) or 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast, experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. To see which interfaces are available, type ? after ipv4-address- and the system displays the object completion options, or run show interface, which lists if-name, if-type, supporting-port, backup-port, protection-mode, vrf, admin-state, oper-state and avail-state.

show route is the consolidated view of every route in use: route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> lists system routes from various sources, with source-protocol naming the origin (OSPF, BGP, static and so on) and special-next-hop none, blackhole or unreachable (default none). The containers are show rib-<rib-name>, with vrf and address-family ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> gives next-hop-address, and show routing gives overall routing information. Hand-typed routes are added with add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> next-hop-address <ip> [interface <name>] [distance <1..255, default 1>] [advertised <true|false, default false>] [special-next-hop blackhole], origin manual or dhcp (default manual); ipv6-static-route is the v6 equivalent.

local-ports and remote-ports belong to the IPsec tunnel: both are Layer 4 port ranges inside a traffic selector. add local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and remote-ports uses the same key, for example add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53 or add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. start may be all, opaque or a port number; stop defaults to 0 and 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. connection-ports is the connectivity object: show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> maps a degree to its dwdm-line port on an RD or ILAx card, which also creates the OMS of that port. degree-number is 1..20 and must not exceed max-degrees; index is 1..2 but is always 1 in 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bidirectional.

take-snapshot makes the copy: take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>], storing the current configuration database in a local backup slot. db-instance is temp (default, used for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage), the automatic onehour, oneday and oneweek, or rollback; type is db-backup (default) or system-backup. It is refused unless a db-passphrase is configured, globally with set security-policies db-passphrase or on the command; it needs a minimum of 40 characters, no dictionary words, Z85 character set. Retaking an existing instance such as oneweek overwrites it. activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>] puts it back; the pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken, and sanity-check-override defaults to false. show database and show database-<database-type> list what exists, with backup-time, description, ne-name and database-state.

activate is a single Operational-mode command whose first parameter selects the function: swimage (activates the currently installable image, implies a system restart; db-action = auto (default) | empty-db | upgrade-db | rollback; label; -f skips confirmation), database (activates the currently inactive database, implies a restart; restart-type cold|warm, default cold; db-instance active/manual/oneday/onehour/oneweek/rollback/temp; db-passphrase 40..200 chars; sanity-check-override false by default), activate-file (file-type, clear-type full|keep-networking|initialize-from-script, default full), location-led (entity = chassis or card, led-mode flash (default) | solid, timeout 0..120 s, default 0 = no timeout, terminate with terminate location-led), loopback (WSS loopback on an nmc-ID), eqpt-fw (resource + fw-image-name), krp, otdr and otdr-fiber-check. For database snapshots there is a separate command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override true|false]; its pre-condition is that a snapshot was already taken with take-snapshot, db-instance defaults to temp and sanity-check-override to false.

capabilities is the per-card one: show capabilities-<name>, where name is the name of the card, retrieves that card's capabilities. l0-capabilities is the photonic one: show l0-capabilities takes no parameters and shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions. oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: show oadm-capabilities [max-degrees] [max-adgs], where max-degrees is the maximum number of degrees (20; degrees exist only on OADM node types, and an ILA node is 0 by convention because it has only 2 fixed directions) and max-adgs is the maximum number of Add/Drop Groups (110, OADM node types only; 0 means not supported). All three are show-only and available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show controller-card-<name> for just the controller: it returns redundancy-status (active | standby | not-in-service, default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status (ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing (default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out, card-not-present), number-of-switchover-events and time-of-last-switchover (both visible only on the active controller), and additional-details (0..128 chars). For any card in the shelf use card: add/set/show/delete card-<name> with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, power-profile, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), oper-state, avail-state, category, last-reboot-reason/time. For what a card model supports use show supported-card-<card-type>: supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands, supported-features.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec one: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (an ethernet facility), enabled (default true), link-security-control must-secure (default) | should-secure, replay-protection enable/disable, replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 (default 0), and the read-only negotiated-cipher-suite. Its cipher terms live in mka-policy (macsec-cipher-suite, confidentiality-offset, sak-rekey-interval 0|30..65535 s, default 30s, key-server-priority), referenced from macsec-mka. secure-entity is the optical/L1 one: add/set/show/delete secure-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (optical-carrier, odu or OTUflex), remote-secure-entity, enabled (default false), re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic | continue-traffic (default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0). Its cipher terms are read-only in secure-entity-sa-proposal: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521.

ase-idler-service is the service-level ASE idler filling function on a card (add/delete/set/show ase-idler-service-<name>): ase-idler-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled) turns ASE filling on the unused and nmc-failed portions of the band spectrum, and ase-idler-state reports ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted or ase-disabled (default ase-disabled); function is idler. ase-idler-source is the hardware pump that produces the ASE signal (set/show only): pump-enable enabled|disabled (default disabled), pump-state, target-output-power -3.00..20.50 dBm (default 13), plus admin-state, supporting-input-port and supporting-output-port; function is ase-idler-source. sw-service does not belong with them at all: it is a software command, show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services, listing software services and containers on the node with state off|ok|fail, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

No, they are the destructive ones. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled|disabled toggles Zero Touch Provisioning; change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, while change-ztp-mode disabled stops ZTP even if it is already in progress. Check the current setting with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode has no parameters and clears the recover-mode flag: it confirms the current configuration as is, re-enables communication with the line cards and may reconfigure traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting. Both are Operational mode and both take -f to skip the confirmation. The carrier-mode commands are harmless read-only queries: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode> and show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> just display capacity, client-mode, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id, status and supported-subtypes.

State: show third-party-app-<app-name> (also show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name>) gives state = running | stopped | failed (default stopped), enable true|false (default false; if enabled the app is started and restarts with the system), plus version, vendor, product, label and information. Firmware side: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> gives file-status valid|invalid|missing, path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version (versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting), present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt (max 80 elements each). Clearing: clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value> clears third party apps. To control rather than clear it, use appctl [app-name=] [command=]restart|netls|exec [target=]<system or chassis/card AID, default system> [parameters=], with up to 50 parameter elements for restart or exec.

Per-session is cli-session-config: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <10..1000, default 40> gives you more rows for that login only; it also carries cli-columns 80..4000 (default 80), interactive-mode true/false (set per CLI session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (default false). The protocol as a whole is cli: set/show cli with enabled (default true; you cannot disable CLI from within a CLI session), port 1..65535 (default 22, ssh), script-dir, default-interactive-mode (default true, affects only newly created sessions) and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns, global effect on all sessions). The two system-configuration ones are config (show config [entity-id|entity-type], displays non-default configuration recursively from the current scope; show config | display commands makes a restore script) and extended-config (add/delete/show extended-config-<name>, a non-standard config whose name must match one known by the system and which introduces exceptional behavior globally).

The generic attribute assignment is set: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [...] [<filter>], operational and candidate mode, at least one attribute-value pair, all pairs on the same managed entity, wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*), ranges card-1-[1..4] and lists, and it prompts for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances (-f forces, -v validates). set-alarm-state is a separate operation: set-alarm-state [state=]<none|ack|close> [[acknowledge-text=]<0..256 chars>] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]<1 to 10 alarm ids>); state is mandatory, acknowledge-text optional. set-time is the time one: set-time [new-time=]<ISO 8601, e.g. 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z or +/-hh:mm>, only applicable when time-source is manual (NTP not enabled); read it back with time. The one ending in -set is named-value-set: add/set/delete/show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <1..1024 chars>].

mc is the Media Channel: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <MHz> upper-frequency <MHz>; the system derives center-frequency and slot-width, and the supporting card must be part of a Degree (not an ADG). nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual carrier slot: add nmc-<name> parent-facility (an MC or an OMS) center-frequency (190650000..196700000 MHz) [width 15000..200000 MHz, default 35000, set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate], plus input/output-attenuation-target (0..15 dB, default max), power-actual-rx/tx and the ASE insertion attributes. The fillers are read-mostly placeholders for unused spectrum: show mc-f-<name> (Media Channel Filler) reports lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width only; nmc-f (Network Media Channel Filler) allows set of admin-state and alarm-report-control and shows alloc-/actual- lower and upper frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state.

The scan is run by activate: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [otdr-file-prefix=] triggers a measurement on the target OTDR port, and activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> triggers a manual OTDR based fiber check (rejected if a manual scan or automatic Raman fiber check is already running; up to 3 tests are executed). You tune it in otdr-ptp: otdr-range auto or 0..300.0 km (set to fiber length plus 10 percent), otdr-pulse-width auto or 10..20000 ns, otdr-measurement-speed fast/medium/slow/precision/auto/high-precision, otdr-ior auto or 1.0..2.0, otdr-fiber-type (auto, SSMF, SMF-ULL, LEAF ...), otdr-resolution auto or 0.4..100.0, otdr-direction-mode (default counter-prop-in-service), peak-power auto or 5..14.5, launching-fiber-length 0..50 m (default 0). The answer comes out of otdr-ptp too: otdr-fiber-break-distance (km, or not-available), otdr-last-measurement and otdr-last-measurement-file (.sor). show otdr-<name> gives live otdr-state (not-available/idle/measuring/finished/fail), otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-port/direction and otdr-error.

For the name server it is the origin attribute on dns-server: add/set/show dns-server-<address> [origin dhcp|manual], default manual. An entry with origin dhcp was assigned by a DHCP server and will be re-learned, so convert it to manual by changing this attribute rather than deleting it. The scope is set globally by dns assignment-method = manual | dhcp | both (default both), together with dns enabled (default true) and dns search (must contain at least one dot; set to an empty string to clear). For the relay there are two levels: dhcp-relay is global, with mode disabled (default) | ipv4 | ipv6 and server-address (at least one IP must be configured when enabled); and if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true|false, default false, enables the relay on that specific interface and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings. A relay does nothing if either the global mode is disabled or the interface flag is still false.

clear [-f] system [type=]<factory-reset | full-wipe | inactive> [[target=]<system, chassis or card AID>] [[restart-behavior=]<restart (default) | shutdown>] does the secure wipe. factory-reset resets the system or a given equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing files and user configurations; it does not take effect for G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E) but is supported on the G30 FRCU controller, and factory-reset with shutdown is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls software on the controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software, and requires a base software reinstall from ONIE to recover. inactive only clears the inactive software partition. The one that leaves logs and performance data behind is clear [-f] database [clear-type=full (default) | keep-networking | initialize-from-script]: it sets the NE database to default and reboots, and explicitly does not wipe logs, PM data or other non-configuration data.

Read show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>: it lists inventory detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration, with hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and detection-timestamp (the last time the Node Controller saw it). Cross-check the cabling with show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port>, which reports src-chassis, dst-chassis and src-chassis-state / dst-chassis-state as node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned. On the chassis object, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller, chassis-role (unknown | main-chassis | sub-chassis), expected-serial-number (which tells the NC the serial number of a sub-chassis) and equipment-discovery-ready, which stays false until all equipment was discovered at startup. To accept the shelf, add chassis-<name> required-type <G31|G32|G34c|G42> expected-serial-number <serial>.

On the amplifier object, control-mode decides it: auto-max-pw (default, the system sets the gain automatically targeting maximum output power) or manual. In manual mode you set gain-target (0..40 dB, default 0.0) and output-voa-attenuation (0..30 dB); in auto mode you can only bias it with gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00 dB, default 0, only on function pa or inline). amp-control-support says whether auto-max-pw is even allowed (auto or manual-only), and gain-range-control follows control-mode (manual forces manual, auto-max-pw forces auto), with gain-range-target standard|low|high. What stops output entirely: amplifier-enable is disabled by default and must be set to enabled, and output power also depends on the OSC signal for node-type ILA and on OMS facilities plus an OXcon for node-type OADM; forced-shutdown true shuts a dual-band amplifier down; admin-state lock; and an input OLOS shutdown, soaked by olos-shutdown-soak-timer (0..2000 ms) unless olos-shutdown-disable is true.

Read the member: show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> state, which is active, standby, available or unknown, alongside role = working or protection and transport-entity. At group level, show protection-group-<name> gives pg-state (no-request, forced-to-working, sf-on-working, wait-to-restore, unavailable (default) and so on), last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. The settings that govern a switch are on protection-group: switching-mode unidirectional (default) | bidirectional, reversion-mode revertive | non-revertive (default), hold-off-timer 0..10000 ms (default 0), wtr-timer 60..720 s (default 300, revertive only), the triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger (all disabled by default), pg-request (clear, manual-to-working/protection, forced-to-working/protection, protection-lockout, exercise) and pg-control-request freeze | clear-freeze. Operate it with protection-switch [operation-type=]force|lockout|manual|release [switch-target=] [protection-group=].

Trigger it with verify [-f] fiber-connection [target-select=]<port-id> [allow-switching]: allow-switching false (default) verifies active paths only, true lets the system switch the OPSM so inactive/protection paths are covered too. The pre-condition is that equipment-policies cable-id-control is set to enabled; the command prompts for confirmation unless -f is given, is non-blocking, and raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued requests finish. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state = idle | running-incl-switching | running-no-switching, and test-progress as a string such as N out of M completed. Read the result with show [-r] cable-id-path-<name>: card-type-a/port-a and card-type-z/port-z (CableID is sourced/terminated only by CAD10A and RD20TM), port-a-to-port-z and port-z-to-port-a path-status enabled|disabled, last-test-status not-verified|pass|fail, last-test-qualifier up-to-date|out-dated, last-test-timestamp and additional-info (Cable-ID-MISMATCH means misconnected fiber, timeout means wrong or loose port). show cable-id lists the entities and terminate cable-id stops running tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by security-policies aaa-authentication-method: local-only (default), local-first-then-remote, remote-first-then-local, or remote-unavailable-then-local. If it is still local-only the node never queries RADIUS. The companion is aaa-authorization-method (local-only default, local-first-then-remote, remote-if-authenticated-else-local, remote-unavailable-then-local); after changing it the user must log out and back in. The server itself is aaa-server-<server-name>: protocol-supported RADIUS (default) or TACACSPLUS, server-address, server-priority 1-10 (order of precedence), server-port default 49, server-port-authentication default 1812, server-port-accounting default 1813, shared-secret (max 64 chars, default sharedkey), source-ip, role-supported authentication/authorization/accounting, enabled true by default. What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout 1..90 s (default 5) and retry 0..5 (default 3), with timeout x (retry + 1) required to be under 5 minutes, plus the fallback chosen in aaa-authentication-method.

For the automation account use ssh-authorized-key: add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label]. Each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication, the user may be local or remote, key-id is a unique name, public-key is up to 2048 characters in OpenSSH/PEM form, and public-key-algorithm is shown as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521 or ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096. Enable it with security-policies ssh-authentication-method = public-key or public-key-or-password (default password). For trusting a remote host the node copies files to, use ssh-known-host: add ssh-known-host-<id> address <hostname/IPv4/IPv6> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value>, with ssh-ed25519 also allowed from R9.0; how strictly it is enforced is set by security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking = strict or relaxed (default relaxed). The node's own identity is ssh-host-key (show only, one per algorithm, auto-generated in the default DB, additional keys added or overwritten via ssh-keygen), showing public-key, fingerprint-algorithm md5|sha256 and fingerprint.

The key agreement policy lives in mka-policy: add/set/show/delete mka-policy-<name> with key-server-priority (used by MKA to select the key server), macsec-cipher-suite (cipher suites for Secure Association Key derivation), confidentiality-offset (number of octets in a frame sent unencrypted) and sak-rekey-interval. The session key rollover is that sak-rekey-interval, the Secure Association Key rekey interval in seconds, range 0|30..65535, default 30s. The policy is bound to the port through macsec-mka: set macsec-mka-<name> mka-policy <name>, plus connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (0..64 chars), psk-lifetime/psk-expiration-warning (1..173 days, default 14), psk-lifetime-enable and the read-only is-key-server and psk-configured-timestamp. Watch the channels with show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index>: sci-tx/sci-rx (16-character hex Secure Channel Identifier), state in-use | not-in-use, association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number. The port-level container is macsec-entity, bound to the ethernet facility.

netconf: set/show netconf, enabled true by default (you cannot disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session), port default 830 over ssh (range 1..65535), hello-timeout 1..3600 s default 2, annotate-cli-name false, static-info-in-notifs up to 10 YANG identifiers. grpc (gNMI/gRPC): set/show grpc, enabled true by default, port default 50051, gnmi-get-encoding-granularity per-path or per-object (default per-object). restconf: enabled true by default, but the transports differ, https-enabled true with https-port 8181, while http-enabled is false by default (and RESTCONF HTTP is not supported in secure mode) with http-port 8080; cookie-timeout 1..300 minutes, default 5. So nothing on that list is off out of the box except RESTCONF over plain HTTP. For reference the CLI itself is set/show cli, enabled true, port 22. All are Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] is Operational mode and asks for confirmation unless -f is given. If you omit resource-id it restarts the active node controller, and if you omit type it does a warm restart by default. warm reboots the processor of a CHM6, UCM4 and similar cards and is non service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes; for XMM4 a warm reboot is non-service-affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, again with connectivity back within five minutes, except that a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting although visibility is lost, while cold reboot of CHM6 or UCM4 is service affecting. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. No, you cannot assume every card behaves alike: not all cards support all restart types. Cards accept cold, warm and shutdown; a card sub-component accepts cold and warm (list them with show card resources); a tom accepts cold only.

Three things must be in place. First the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <enabled|disabled>, which is disabled by default; on enabling, existing TOMs are not retro-configured, templates only apply from that moment onward, and on disabling existing serdes configuration is kept. Second a template keyed to the part number: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <1..16 chars>] [card-types-applicable] [ports-applicable], where ports-applicable defaults to all ports (or a list of up to 20 port names such as T1, T10). Third the values: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<entry-name> value <value>, one entry per serdes parameter, for example RxAmplitude, RxEQ, TxEQ, TxEQAdaptive, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor. The card must also support it, show supported-card-<card-type> support-serdes-config must be true. Then when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in the template is applied automatically; manual serdes settings are kept even if they deviate, swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets serdes and re-applies the new template, and apply-template forces re-application.

ots (Optical Transport Section) represents the fiber span itself: fiber-type-tx/rx (default SSMF), fiber-length-tx/rx auto or 0..500.0 km, span-loss-transmit/receive 0..80 dB, span-loss-derived-rx/tx measured from OSC, span-loss-reference configured|measured (default measured), external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB, target-power-setting manual|auto|auto-plan (default auto) and laser-safety-mode OPLM or APSD. oms (Optical Multiplex Section) is the multiplexed band on a degree: grid-mode flexible (default) or fixed-50G-96ch / fixed-75G-64ch / fixed-100G-48ch / fixed-150G-40ch, monitoring-mode, attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx auto by default, lower-frequency 191300000 and upper-frequency 196150000 MHz, band-allowed/actual/target, assigned-degree. ops (Optical Physical Section) is the per-port physical section: role tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, input-psd-profile -30..-6 dBm/12.5GHz (default -6), port-expansion no|y-cable. osc (Optical Supervisory Channel) carries the supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE for HSC OLS, osc-control auto|manual (default auto), target-output-power -2.5..4.5 dBm, voa-attenuation-target-rx 0..30 dB (default 10), l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6.

The behaviour is configured on the tributary client termination, trib-ptp, with tributary-disable-action: it says what the NE does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais and send-nos (G30 only). So by default the node turns the client-facing laser off. Delay it with tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it is only applicable when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, holding the optical signal until the timer expires. Related switches on the same object are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (BERSD-ODU triggers ALS, default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true by default: an incoming client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side, otherwise it triggers an egress TDA action). Set it with, for example, set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off.

The system creates the high-order layer for you: the high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH (super-channel) is created, so on a CHM6 with an OTU configured use 'show odu' to check it exists. The odu command carries the pre-condition that the super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added. So you add super-channel-<name> (carriers, carrier-mode), then hand-create the low order ODUs with 'add odu-<name> odu-type <ODU4i|ODUflexi|ODU4|ODUflex|ODU0|ODU1|ODU2|ODU2e> parent-odu <HO-ODU> time-slots/opucn-time-slots trib-port-number', then the xcon. Line OTUs are added with a parent, e.g. 'add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1'. Which is which is visible in the managed-by attribute (system or user, default system on facilities); only user-created facilities can be user deleted. The class attribute reports high-order, low-order or mapped.

The bit error rate test is the 'bert' command (Operational Mode): 'bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=egress test-duration=10', plus bert stop/get/delete. test-signal-type is none, PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV or scrambled-idles (100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV); monitoring type adds fec-frames. test-duration is 10 s minimum up to 1000 hrs, 0 means indefinite. Test patterns are injected per facility via test-signal-type / test-signal-direction / test-signal-monitoring on odu-diagnostics and ethernet (none, PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV; direction ingress, egress or both; monitoring default false). Loop the signal back with the loopback attribute on otu, odu, ethernet or optical-carrier: none (default), facility or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

Each end needs a secure-entity bound to the local facility and pointed at its far-end peer: 'add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <facility> remote-secure-entity <AID>' where remote-secure-entity is the AID of the remote optical carrier (1830 GX G40), the remote ODU (1830 GX G30) or the remote OTUFlex (CHM7/CHM7X L1 service encryption). The enabled switch defaults to false and must be set true. Tunable policy: re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic), traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0), alarm-report-control default Inhibited. The SA proposal is fixed: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521. Certificates must already be imported: the peer-certificate is the trusted remote peer certificate for the L1 encryption secure application, and the local-certificate is the NE's own identity assigned to the secure-application.

The 'telemetry' command configures persistent and dynamic telemetry ('show telemetry', 'set telemetry id <string 0..4096>'); the object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. 'show subscriptions' lists the subscriptions. Per subscription, 'show current-subscription-<subscription-name>' gives related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding (json, bytes, proto, ascii, json-ietf; default json-ietf), transfer-mode (stream default, once, poll), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one watches comes from 'show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>': subscription-path, subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode (target-defined default, on-change, sample), sample-interval (default 0; a target-defined stream is auto-adjusted from 0 to 10 seconds), heartbeat-interval (default 0; auto-adjusted to 20 seconds) and suppress-redundant (default true).

At rest the configuration database is encrypted; 'show db-protection-scheme' reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode, 64-byte block), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup / failed-on-bootup / disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which is changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before you can take a copy, the db-passphrase used for DB snapshot encryption must be configured, either globally with 'set security-policies db-passphrase' (string 40..200) or supplied on the command as 'take-snapshot db-passphrase=***'. It requires a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and special characters follow the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. Then 'take-snapshot [db-instance=temp|manual|onehour|oneday|oneweek|rollback] [description=]' (type db-backup default, or system-backup); list results with 'show database'.

Start at the RIB. 'show rib-<rib-name>' lists each RIB by its name key, with the vrf it is bound to and its address-family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast); all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, e.g. 'show rib-IPv4'. Then 'show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>' tells you if the prefix made it in and where it came from: source-protocol (OSPF, BGP, static, etc.) and special-next-hop, which is none (normal routes), blackhole or unreachable, default none; for blackhole and unreachable no next-hop is created under the route. 'show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface>' gives the next-hop-address and outgoing interface, e.g. 'show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN'. Which instance it landed in comes from 'show vrf-<name>' (type mgmt or internal, chassis-name); 'show routing' is the umbrella view.

Password acceptance is governed by security-policies. strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum length 8, at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and the user name cannot be part of the password; disabled drops all of these except a 1-character minimum. minimum-password-length is 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of the previous 5 passwords, with password-history-size 1..200, default 5. These only affect newly defined passwords. Lockout is per user: max-invalid-login is the maximum consecutive invalid login attempts before the account is suspended, range 0..255, default 5, and suspension-time is 0..1440 minutes, default 5; user-status reports lockout, and failed-logins resets to zero on a successful login. security-policies also has disable-user-lockout. To clear a stuck session, run 'show session' for the session-id (<ip-address>:<port>) then 'kill-session <session-id>'; you cannot kill your own session, use exit.

Untouched syslog defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Console logging is off by default: log-console enabled defaults to false. Local files: log-file number-of-files is the maximum number of log files retained, range 1..20, default 10, and when rotating due to max-file-size the oldest files are discarded beyond that count; max-file-size is 1..30 megabytes, default 30; source-facilities defaults to all; severity is informational and above by default; the default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Remote servers default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, origin manual, enabled true. The single switch that turns off everything remote is 'set syslog remote-logging-switch false' - if false, all remote logging destinations are disabled.

What is raised now: 'show current-alarms' (number-of-alarms, last-changed), 'show alarms', and 'show alarm-<alarm-id>' for detail (perceived-severity, reported-time, service-affecting, alarm-category, corrective-action, operator-state/text/name). Manual clearing is 'clear [-f] alarm <alarm-type> [resource=...]'. Most alarms have automatic raise and clear criteria; only a small subset must be acknowledged and cleared by hand, and you find them with 'show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true'. This applies only to system-wide/global alarms not associated with any particular resource. 'set-alarm-state <none|ack|close> [acknowledge-text=] (all-alarms | alarm-id-list=<up to 10 ids>)' changes the operator state. Whether inhibiting reporting drops the already-raised alarms is decided by 'set alarm-control arc-behavior': clear-alarms clears the current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, leave-alarms (the default) leaves them raised.

The Equipment dashboard shows the sensors: 'status equipment' lists the chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, and per equipment the temperature sensors and power values plus presence, oper-state and alarms (for example 'temp 25C | power 2.1/4400 W' on a chassis and 'temp 25C' per card). Narrow it by supplying the chassis id as the filter, e.g. 'status equipment 5'; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so it is either all chassis or exactly one. To get down to one slot use the PM data with a filter, e.g. 'show pm card-1-7', which reports real-time temperature (C) per resource with instant/avg/min/max. Physically the state is reflected in the LEDs: 'show leds', 'show led status' or 'show led-<location>/<name> status', with values not-available (default), off, green, flashing-green, yellow, flashing-yellow, amber, flashing-amber, red, flashing-red, cycling and cycling-with-off.

'show ots-<name>' tells you what the line is doing: span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx are the measured span loss based on OSC including losses external to the fiber, 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS; span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive are the configured fiber losses (0..80 dB, default 0; 99 dB also means not configured on receive, and changing span-loss-receive is traffic affecting). span-loss-reference selects which is used, configured or measured, default measured. span-loss-alarm-threshold (0..80 dB, 99 dB, default 99) is set autonomously by the system, is persistent across warm/cold boot, and in measured mode can be forced to update with the update command. span-loss-aging-margin-rx is 0..10.00 dB, default 1.0. What the amplifier is compensating with comes from 'show amplifier-<name>': gain-target and gain-operating (0..40 dB), gain-range-actual, gain-adjustment (-20.00..20.00), input-power-mon and output-power-mon (-99.00..99.00 dBm), tilt-actual and tilt-target, control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, span-loss-control enabled by default, and control-state (converged, fine-tuning, adjusting, stopped).

The chain is trib-ptp (the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver and the immediate protocol layer) into the client protocol facility, ethernet or a client otu, into a low order odu, tied across the node by an xcon (source and destination end-points, payload-type 100GBE/400GBE/OTU4/100G/ODU2/ODU2e, payload-treatment transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen or regen-switching, network-mapping naming the server layer). The low order ODU sits under a parent-odu high-order ODUCn/ODUCni, which sits under the line otu (OTUCn) and its flexo-group, which binds carriers. From there it becomes optical: line-ptp / super-channel-group, super-channel, optical-carrier, optical-channel. The handover is at line-ptp and optical-carrier: optical-carrier owns frequency, wavelength, tx-power, modulation-format and baud-rate, and line-ptp's line-system-mode (openwave) is the L1 to L0 power control towards the line-system card. Walk it with 'show facilities' and each object's supporting-facilities and supported-facilities.

No, they are two different knobs. A counter crossing a limit is a PM threshold crossing: 'add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]' (numbers, or na, or not-supported; default na), and the TCA must actually be supervised, which is 'set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true' per instance or default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> for newly created resources. How loudly an existing fault is reported is alarm severity: 'set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>', for example 'set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor', or 'set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <...>'. 'show alarm-inventory-<alarm-type> default-severity' gives the system default for that alarm type.

Stop it reporting with the card's own alarm-report-control: 'set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited' (values allowed and inhibited). Each facility on it has the same attribute, defaulting to allowed on odu, otu, ethernet, ots, trib-ptp, line-ptp, flexo-group and so on, so inhibit those too if you want silence at facility level. You can also put the card into maintenance with 'set card-<name> admin-state maintenance' (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), which shows up in avail-state as maintenance. What happens to the alarms it has already raised is decided system-wide by 'set alarm-control arc-behavior': clear-alarms clears the current alarms when ARC is set to inhibit, while leave-alarms, which is the default, leaves the current alarms in a raised mode. The related alarm-soaking-behavior switch is automatic (default) or no-soak.

A secure application is one that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity, and the certificate it presents is its active-certificate-id: 'set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <cert>' (a list, string 0..128, e.g. 'set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY'). 'show secure-application-<id>' returns type (server or client), active-certificate-id, in-use (the active certificate, a leafref to active-certificate-id), status (enabled or disabled) and verify-client-cert (disabled by default, or required for TLS Mutual Authentication; changes apply only to new TLS connections). Before it will come up the certificate must be imported in PEM format: 'import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM> [passphrase]', plus its CA chain with 'import-certificate trusted-certificate ... [-i]' (-i pulls intermediates from a bundle; roots are installed individually). 'show local-certificate-<id> status' must read valid, not pending-import, expired, revoked or untrusted. For L1 encryption the far-end identity is a peer-certificate.

Pipe the show pm output through the display filter: 'show pm <command flag> | display csv' produces CSV data importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; 'display xml' and 'display json' are also available. Restrict it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter for period, e.g. 'show pm pm-15min | display csv', and add other content filters such as parameter, resource, resource-type or AID (use 'show pm <tab>' for the full list of supported filters). Bin 0 is the current data and bins 1 to n are history, and the bin-to-timestamp mapping is printed with history output. Useful flags: -t for standard table format, -n=<number-of-records> for the maximum records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> to page through, -st= and -et= for a timestamp window (format 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00), -sbin= and -ebin= for a bin window (default first bin 0, all bins), and -i=<chassis-name>, which may only be given once per command.

Use the PM catalog: 'show pm-catalog <string>' where the string is the catalog name. For example 'show pm-catalog parameter-undersized' returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The equivalent per-parameter lookup is 'show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]', for example 'show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds', or 'show pm-parameter' for the full list of PM parameters. Both give you the same two facts about the counter name: what unit it is expressed in and whether it is a counter or a gauge.

Turn off data-supervision for that resource with pm-control: 'set pm-control <entity> data-supervision false', for example 'set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false'. The entity is the resource to be configured, and data-supervision is real-time data supervision for that resource, valid values true and false, default true. 'show pm-control' lists the configuration for all currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The per-instance equivalent is 'set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false' (true/false, default true), which you can read back with 'show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision' along with resource-type, AID and real-time-data-last-reset. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. pm-control-entry sets the PM configuration for one particular resource, for one particular period, direction and location, so the key itself gives you exactly that scope: 'set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true', for example 'set pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true'. period is the PM time period (pm-15min, pm-24h), direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, and location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all. The same entry also carries data-supervision (true/false). 'show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [supported-parameters] [data-supervision] [tca-supervision]' reads it back; supported-parameters lists the PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements.

Query the parameter object: 'show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]', for example 'show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds', or 'show pm-parameter' for the whole list. type is the type of PM parameter and is either counter or gauge. units is one of na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors or MHz. Example output for pm-parameter-undersized is units packets, type counter. The same two attributes come back from 'show pm-catalog <catalog-name>'. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use the PM profile's global switch: 'set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled'. The parameter provides a way to globally enable PM data-supervision without having to toggle it individually. Its two values are auto-enabled, which globally enables the PM data-supervision flag, and manual, which is the default and means the data-supervision flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry or directly per pm-control-entry. Read it back with 'show pm-profile'. The pm-profile object contains information on all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration; it is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the per-resource-type default on pm-profile-entry, which holds the PM configuration per resource type: 'set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true'. default-data-supervision determines, for newly created resources of this type, whether they have PM data supervision automatically enabled or not (true or false). The companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision on newly created resources. In the key, direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all, and period is the PM time period. Read it back with 'show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision] [default-tca-supervision]'. Note that pm-profile global-data-supervision must be left at manual for these per-type defaults to be the controlling setting.

Read real-time-data-last-reset on the pm-resource for that port: 'show pm-resource-<resource> real-time-data-last-reset', for example 'show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9'. The attribute is the date and time of the last real time data reset for this resource, in date-and-time format, and if the data was never reset it is the date and time of that resource's creation. The same show also returns resource-type, AID (string 1..64), real-time-supervision (true/false, default true) and the list of pm-control-entry children such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. Clearing is done with 'clear pm real-time' plus optional resource, resource-type, period, location, direction or AID filters to narrow the target.

Create a pm-threshold keyed to that instance: 'add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]', for example a high limit on errored-seconds for one facility's 24-hour ingress near-end bin. resource is the existing system resource instance ID, period is the PM time period (pm-15min, pm-24h), direction is ingress, egress, all or na with default all, location is all, na, near-end or far-end with default all, and parameter is the PM parameter identifier, which can be a counter or a gauge. low-threshold and high-threshold take a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na, or not-supported, and default to na. Use set to change it, 'show pm-threshold-.../<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold]' to read it and delete to remove it. For the threshold to raise a TCA, tca-supervision must be true on the matching pm-control-entry.

Use the PM threshold profile, which holds PM configuration per parameter for a resource type: 'show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]'. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, and min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values for it, which is the range you are allowed to configure. All of these take a number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na, or not-supported. low-threshold and high-threshold are the configured values and are the only settable ones: 'set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200'. In the key, direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all), location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all).

Use the clock commands. To change the zone: set clock timezone <value>, for example set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]. The timezone list runs from International Date Line West[GMT-12:00] through Kiritimati[GMT+14:00] plus Universal-Time-Coordinated, which is the default. To see where the time comes from: show clock time-source. Values are ntp (the NE uses NTP for synchronization) and manual (the NE uses its internal clock); the default is manual. show clock also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, which reports the last jump as <time1> to <time2> and ignores jumps under 10 seconds. If DNS is not properly configured, show clock can take up to 2 minutes to respond. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Yes. Use set ne node-type OADM. node-type takes ILA, OADM or XPDR, and it can only be set or changed on a 1830 GX G34c chassis, where the default is ILA. G31 and G32 chassis support only OADM, and G42 defaults to XPDR. Support for OADM on G34c starts with R7.0; in R6.x the G34c was ILA only. Pre-conditions to move to OADM: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be ila-with-equalization or not-monitored, meaning no spectrum (or ochm) objects may exist, and no direction-* may exist. Going the other way, to configure ILA, no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be intrusive (no RD or PAx card can exist), and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc may exist. Note that G34c slte mode under l0-mode-op is supported only when node-type is ILA.

show ne-function. It displays the NE generic functions in a single list, covering the node's directions and amplifiers, for example direction-1 through direction-8, amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and the ne-function entry itself. The command is show only; there is no add, set or delete form and it takes no parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the ntp object: set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true. ntp-enabled is true/false with a default of true; ntp-auth-enabled is true/false with a default of false, so authentication has to be turned on explicitly. The third attribute is assignment-method, values manual, dhcp or both, default both, which selects whether the system uses manually configured values, DHCP-supplied values, or both. show ntp returns ntp-enabled, ntp-auth-enabled, assignment-method and ntp-active-server (the currently active NTP server). The ntp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually added or deleted. Authentication then needs a key: add ntp-key-<key-id> with is-trusted true, and point the server at it with the auth-key-id attribute on ntp-server-<ip-address>. Access mode: Operational and Candidate Configuration.

NTP keys are managed with add/set/show/delete ntp-key-<key-id>. key-type is the hash algorithm used for NTP message digest computation and accepts sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 and md5; there is no default, and key-type is mandatory on add. key-id is a number in the range 1..65534. key-value is a string of length 8..40, also mandatory on add. is-trusted marks the key as a trusted NTP key, values true/false, default false. Example: add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The key is then bound to a server through the auth-key-id attribute of ntp-server-<ip-address>.

Yes. The origin attribute on the ntp-server object exists for exactly this: a user can convert a DHCP configured NTP entry into a manually configured one by changing the attribute. Run set ntp-server-<ip-address> origin manual. Values are dhcp (the address was assigned to this system by a DHCP server) and manual (the address was manually configured); the default is manual. The ip-address key can be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS domain name. The other ntp-server attributes are auth-key-id (uint32 or not-applicable, default not-applicable), label (0..256 characters), admin-state (lock, unlock or maintenance, default unlock) and alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited, default allowed); oper-state and avail-state are show only. Related: the ntp object's assignment-method (manual, dhcp, both, default both) controls which configured values the system uses.

Use show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>, for example show ntp-server-status-172.19.13.218. The key field is reach: it is an 8-bit shift register with the most recent probe in the 2^0 position, and the value 377 means all the recent probes have been answered. Also available: when (seconds since the last packet was received), poll (polling interval in seconds), delay (path delay to the server in ms), offset (clock offset to the peer in ms), jitter (path jitter in ms), stratum of the remote peer, refid (reference clock type or address, string 1..32), type (local, unicast, multicast or broadcast), auth-status (ok, yes, bad or none, default none) and condition (string 1..16, with values such as sys.peer, reject or candidate). Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The restart command syntax is restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>], and if <type> is omitted a warm start is done by default. warm reboots the processor of the CHM6, UCM4 and similar cards and is non service affecting; the system regains connectivity within five minutes, and on an XMM4 a warm reboot is non-service affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; connectivity returns within five minutes; a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting but visibility is lost, while cold reboot of CHM6 or UCM4 is service affecting. There is also shutdown, which gracefully shuts down the card. Restartable entities: card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold); not all cards support all types. If <resource-id> is omitted the active controller card is restarted. The command asks for confirmation unless -f is given. List sub-components with show card resources.

set-time is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled. Check with show clock time-source (values ntp or manual, default manual) and show ntp ntp-enabled; if NTP is on, disable it with set ntp ntp-enabled false before setting the clock by hand. The new time uses a format derived from ISO 8601 with combined date and time, for example set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z where Z is the UTC timezone; a non-UTC zone is allowed by supplying +/-hh:mm instead of Z, for example set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00. Syntax is set-time [new-time=]<value>, with -h for help. Access mode is Operational Mode. Read the current system time back with the time command, which reports it in the system configured timezone rather than the timezone used in the set-time command.

Yes: status equipment. It is one of the dashboards of the status command, whose syntax is status [[dashboard=]<system | equipment | L0-oxcon | L0-ocm | L1-traffic>] [[filter=]<value>]. The Equipment dashboard summarises all equipment in the system with relevant details like temperature and power usage: the list of chassis, the cards per chassis and their subtype, the toms per card, per-equipment temperature sensors and power values, plus generic status covering presence or absence, oper-state and alarms. The default scope is the entire network element. On large NEs the output can be filtered per chassis by giving the chassis id, for example status equipment 5; only existing chassis ids are accepted and wildcards are not supported, so you get either all chassis or exactly one. Output uses a check mark for oper-state enabled, admin-state unlocked or no alarms, a cross for oper-state disabled, and a padlock for admin-state lock. Access mode is Operational mode.

Use clear [-f] system [[action=]<value>] [[restart-behavior=]<value>] [type=]<value> [[target=]<value>] with type factory-reset, for example clear system factory-reset shutdown. clear system wipes the system or a specific instance back to factory configuration and does a secure wipe of the system data. factory-reset resets the system or a particular equipment to factory configuration, stopping target traffic services and removing the respective files and user configurations, which may imply loss of connectivity. Limits: factory-reset does not take effect for 1830 GX G30 Optical Carrier-Cards (OCC2T, OCC2E), it is supported for the G30 controller card (FRCU), and clear system factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards. target may be the entire system or a specific chassis or card AID; with no target the entire system is cleared. restart-behavior is a standard restart (default) or shutdown, in which case the system does not restart afterwards.
