Use set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>] and read it back with show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address]. mode takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6 and defaults to disabled, so relay is off until you change it. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses, IPv4 or IPv6; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. You can do both in one command, for example set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3, or just the mode with set dhcp-relay mode ipv4. This is the global setting; individual interfaces are enabled separately with set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, which obeys these global dhcp-relay settings. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes. The dns object has an assignment-method attribute that indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts DNS servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and view with show dns [assignment-method] [enabled] [search]. enabled is a true/false flag indicating whether DNS is enabled, default true. search is the DNS search suffix name, string 0..64, and it must contain at least a single dot; set it to an empty string to clear it. Per-server origin is tracked separately on dns-server, where origin is dhcp or manual. Examples: set DNS enabled true and show DNS.

Add one with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. Remove with delete dns-server-<address>, change with set dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], and inspect with show dns-server-<address> [origin]. The origin attribute is how you tell where an entry came from: dhcp indicates a DNS address that was assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address was manually configured. The default is manual. You can also use it in the other direction: the user can convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object, which is per interface. Syntax: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled <value>] and show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, string 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled takes true or false and defaults to false, so relay is off on an interface until you enable it. It enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface only and obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global set dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (default disabled) with at least one server-address configured for it to do anything. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true, and read it back with show if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

By default it is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [...], ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and both default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode takes unknown, protected or unprotected and defaults to protected (protected means backed by redundant ports, unprotected means no port redundancy); protection-state is the read-only current state and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: admin-state unlock, oper-state disabled, alarm-report-control allowed, proxy-arp-enabled false (applicable only to the DCN interface), if-dhcp-relay false. if-type is show-only and takes ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc. Note that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface.

Yes, that is exactly what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings certain destinations and the result takes action on configured static routes. Create it with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into failed state and takes none or withdraw, defaulting to withdraw, so route withdrawal is the default behaviour. static-route is the list of connected static routes for the instance, maximum 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (IPv4 or IPv6). next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the monitoring instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is the time between two consecutive pings, 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10 percent steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled defaults to true. The affected route reports monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>. Read it with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Type ? after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. netmask is the subnet expressed as a netmask and only valid netmasks are allowed. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. Certain addresses are disallowed: those beginning with 0 (current network), those beginning with 127 (loopback), and those beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). origin is show-only and takes static, dhcp or auto-config, default static, where static means configured through NETCONF or the CLI, dhcp means assigned by a DHCP server, and auto-config means created by autoconfiguration. Examples: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0' and add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Syntax: add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. For a discard route, use special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole). Blackhole static routes exist because routes advertised to an external AS must be in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, not by BGP itself; for routes not present in the IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Other attributes: advertised true/false, default false, which when set advertises the route in the routing protocol and, for OSPF, as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR; origin manual or dhcp, default manual; the interface VRF must match the static-route VRF. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

Nearly, but the subnet is given as a prefix length rather than a netmask. Use add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, with show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin] and delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed. Note that IPv6 /127 subnets are currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and do not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. origin is show-only and takes static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. Use ? after ipv6-address- to list the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Pass interface DCN-B on the route. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Syntax: add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. The VRF bound to the interface must match the VRF given on the static route. Example: add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B, versus the primary case add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN. Defaults: distance 1 (range 1..255), advertised false, origin manual (or dhcp), special-next-hop blackhole, monitoring-state unmonitored. Access: Operational mode and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each one must have a distinct management address type (subtype) and management address (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to that LLDP neighbor. direction is ingress or egress. address is a string 0..64 identifying the management address component of the remote system, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface type associated with the address and takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. if-id is the integer interface number for that management address component on the remote system. address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity associated with the address advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in scope and key. management-address covers the addresses learned per direction, keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, so it includes a direction component of ingress or egress. management-address-local reports the management address information from the local LLDP ports and drops that component: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>. Both accept [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid], both are read-only, and both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. if-subtype takes unknown (interface not known), if-index (identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object) or system-port-number (identifier based on the system port numbering convention). On management-address-local the address-oid field, a string 0..128, is currently an empty string. Example: show management-address-local.

Yes, it is the use-as-source attribute of the networking object. Set it with set networking [use-as-source <value>] and read it with show networking [use-as-source]. use-as-source names the interface to use as the source address and takes a string of length 0..64; no default is defined. Example: set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and show networking to view the current networking information. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

show networking-services. It is used to show the list of network services and takes no command parameters, so there is nothing to qualify or filter. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This is distinct from the networking command (set networking / show networking), which handles the use-as-source attribute naming the interface to use as source address.

Next hop data is modelled under the RIB because each entry in 'show next-hop' represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family. For each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so the RIB is what ties a next hop to an instance and family. Syntax: show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]. rib-name is a string of length 1..64 with pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface reference (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN.

Use clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>. The clear ospf command removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The instance id is supplied as <instance> and is a string. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted to confirm. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: clear ospf 1. Note that the ospf-instance command page also points to clear for removing an OSPF instance from the configuration asynchronously.

No. The ospf-area commands are add/set/show/delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], and the only permitted value for ospf-area-type is normal, which is also the default. There is no stub or NSSA option. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. The pre-condition is that the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use ospf-area-range, which summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask, and it is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only. Syntax: add|set ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>], plus show and delete on the same AID. The prefix may be an IPv4 prefix (length up to 32) or an IPv6 prefix (length up to 128) in canonical form. The advertise parameter takes true or false and defaults to true, where false hides the range. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true.

Yes. ospf-instance takes a version parameter with values ospfv2 or ospfv3, defaulting to ospfv2, and version is only settable at add time (add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <value> [version <value>] [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>]). The router id is controlled by router-id-mode, values manual or use-loopback, default use-loopback; with manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad. Pre-condition: if router-id-mode is use-loopback then an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. instance-id is uint8 0..255 and description is a string of length 0..128. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name> the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related defaults: retransmission-interval 5 seconds (2..3600), transmit-delay 1 second (1..450), ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto). Authentication is available: ospf-auth-enable is true/false, default false, and is only of relevance for ospfv2 or ospfv3; ospf-auth-algorithm is none or HMAC_SHA_256, default HMAC_SHA_256, and ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string of length 0..256, both only of relevance for ospfv2. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must be present.

Use show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority]. The state values are: down (initial state, no Hello packets received from the neighbor), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional communication established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor (DBD) packets containing LSA headers), loading (routers exchange full Link State information based on DBDs), and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Access mode is Operational Mode. An OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use ospfv3-ipsec-security-association: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], with matching set, show and delete. The integrity-algorithm values are AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96; it is mandatory on add and has no default. ipsec-protocol indicates ESP or AH but only ESP is offered, default ESP; ipsec-mode supports only transport, default transport. spi is a unique uint32 in range 256..4294967295. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w sets a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the payload octets excluding headers, default 56 plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest can be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. Example: ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3.

Use show protocols, which lists all protocol information in one place, then drill into any one with show protocols <name>. The selectable protocols are ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. Each sub-view shows its own settings, for example ssh (enabled, port 8022, host keys, pre/post-login messages), cli (enabled true, port 22, script-dir /storage/scripts), serial-console (global-switch, global-timeout 60 minutes), netconf (enabled true, port 830), restconf (https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root /restconf), grpc (enabled true, port 50051), snmp (enabled true, port 161, snmp-engine-id) and http-file-server (http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base /transfer). Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family. rib-name is a string of length 1..64, vrf is a leafref to ../../vrf/name giving the VRF the RIB is bound to, and address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show rib-IPv4 views the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key.

Use show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. The route command shows the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static route, and source-protocol is the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP or static. special-next-hop indicates any special treatment for IPv4/IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring: none (no special treatment, used for all normal routes, and the default), blackhole (for blackhole routes no next-hop is created under route) and unreachable (for unreachable routes no next-hop is created under route). rib-name is a string of length 1..64. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show route.

Yes. show routing displays routing information. It takes no parameters at all, so it is issued exactly as show routing. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detailed views, the related commands are show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for the RIB entries per address family, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for the system routes and their source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address] for next hops, and show vrf-<name> for the routing instances.

show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface> shows supporting interface information, that is, which underlying interface supports a given interface. The parameters are name, the name of the interface, a string; and interface, a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface given as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. Both are used only in show. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

traceroute follows a maximum of 30 hops by default: -m=<hopcnt> sets the maximum number of hops (max time-to-live value), uint8 in range 1..255, default 30. The VRF defaults to MGMT: -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF to be used and if not provided defaults to MGMT. Syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]. -w is the timeout in seconds, uint16 range 1..10, default 2. -i=<interface> sets the source interface, otherwise the interface is selected according to the routing table; the interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. pktsize is the total probe packet size, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). Example: traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description], which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. chassis-name is the associated chassis name for that VRF. name is a string of length 0..32, type is mgmt (Management VRF) or internal (Internal VRF), and description is a string of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. All four parameters are used in show only. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show vrf-MGMT displays the Management VRF attributes.

activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>] activates the currently installable software image, and a successful swimage activation implies a system restart. db-action specifies the expected database operation: auto (the system default behavior, the default value), empty-db (activate with an empty database), upgrade-db (activate by upgrading the current database) and rollback (roll back to the previous active software image). If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless -f is given, you must confirm the activation when prompted. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name; if not specified the currently installable image is used. Access mode is Operational Mode. Example: activate swimage db-action=empty-db.

No, only a single location led test can be running at a time. Use activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>], where entity is a chassis or a card. led-mode is flash (default), an amber light flashing at 1Hz, usually for LED location, or solid, a steady amber light, usually for lamp test; when lamp test is enabled all chassis LEDs light amber. To turn it off, use terminate location-led [entity=]<value>, or set timeout, a number in range 0..120 seconds, default 0, which means no timeout so the function runs until terminated. The timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so use terminate there. Not all cards support the Location LED test. Example: activate location-led card-1-1.

Use bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>. It bootstraps a neighbor NE by establishing a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisioning the initial administrator account, for commissioning an OSC peer NE that has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either with local-port, the supporting-port of a MGMT vrf osc-eth interface (same value as in show interface, e.g. 1-1-dwdm-line1), which the system maps to the OCE netdev OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id> and resolves to the peer IPv6 link-local address via get_osc_neighbors.sh (if resolution fails the RPC is rejected), or with neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address including zone, string length 7..256 matching pattern fe80:.*. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and follows local user naming rules; new-password may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a $6$ SHA512 hash. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration.

Type cancel-upgrade. The command cancels any active upgrade in progress. Full syntax is cancel-upgrade [-h], where -h is the only flag and displays help for this command; there are no other parameters and no entity or AID to supply. Access mode is Operational mode. Pre-condition: an upgrade must be in progress for this command to execute successfully, so if nothing is running the command will not execute successfully. Example given in the guide: cancel-upgrade, which cancels any active upgrade.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so re-enabling it on an in-service node wipes the configuration back to factory defaults and reboots. Syntax: change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>, where ztp-mode takes enabled or disabled and has no default, and -f forces the command without confirmation, so leave -f off to get the confirmation prompt. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. The current ZTP mode is displayed with show ztp. Access mode is Operational mode.

Use show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name> [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status] (variants also accept <card-name>.<slot-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name> or <name>). Compare fw-version, the current version of the firmware, against expected-fw-version, the expected version; both are strings of length 0..32. fw-status gives the verdict directly: current (current firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) and unavailable (information on firmware status is currently unavailable), which is also the default. fw-name is a string of length 0..32. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: show current-fw or show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1.

download supports filetype values crl (a Certificate Revocation List in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (passphrase protected X.509 in PKCS#12, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 in PKCS#12), script (a CLI script from a remote server), swimage (a manifest file plus all files belonging to a SW image), and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place, so no local location is needed; use show transfer to see the default storage directory. Only filetype file accepts destination, which may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp.

Use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which retrieves information about downloaded image files. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file and its information, a string of length 0..256; name is the name of the downloaded software image, a string of length 0..256; and signature is the downloaded software image file signature, a string of length 0..1024. All parameters are used in show only. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Issue show downloaded-image to list all downloaded software image files.

show downloads is the command that shows a list of downloads. Its syntax is exactly show downloads and it has no parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For image-specific detail on what was pulled down, use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which reports the manifest file, the downloaded software image name and its file signature. For a transfer still running, in particular one started asynchronously with download -a, use show transfer-status filetype to see the current state, and show transfer to see the default storage directory.

Use the `file` command in Operational mode: `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`. Supported operations are rename (renames a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), view (listing for a file or directory), sha256sum (SHA256 hash checksum) and md5sum (md5 hash checksum). new-file-path applies only to rename and follows the pattern '[A-Za-z0-9 \-/\.]*'. The result attribute reports the file operation result. Access is not unlimited: file system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`, `file view /tmp`. Separately, `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` removes one particular file, with filetype krp, script or swimage.

`file` is the fuller command: operation values rename, delete, view, sha256sum and md5sum, plus a result attribute, and it is paired with `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` for clearing krp, script or swimage files. `file-operation` is the reduced form, syntax `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>`, and it supports only rename, delete and view; it has no checksum operations and no result parameter. Both take file-path (path to the file) and new-file-path (new path, used for rename) as strings, and both run in Operational mode. Use `file` when you also need sha256sum/md5sum hashes or file clearing.

`add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`, with `set`, `show file-server-<name>`, `show file-servers` and `delete file-server-<name>`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http and https; ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false, and 'file' means local storage including USB and requires initial-path to be provided. server-address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a domain name. server-port is optional: if not provided the default for the selected protocol is used. name is 0...64 chars, user-name 0..64, password 0...128, initial-path 0...256, label 0...256. Example: `add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'`.

Use `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]`. name is the file type for which the transfer happened. last-completion-status gives the last transfer status, last-transfer is the last transfer start timestamp as date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), last-duration is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and last-operation is the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. The command runs in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For per-operation detail including progress and byte counts, use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>` instead.

Yes, but HTTP is off by default. Use `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]` and `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled (the master switch for file server access) defaults to true. http-enabled is true/false with default false; https-enabled is true/false with default true. http-port defaults to 8980 and https-port defaults to 8981, both plain numbers. url-base is the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application, a string of 1..100 characters, default /transfer, and is read-only via show.

Use the manifest commands, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` gives the manifest itself: manifest-signature is a hex-string 0..1024, downloaded-on is the download timestamp in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and information is a string 0..256. `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` gives each package: state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version is 0..64 chars, description 0..512. `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` lists included firmware versions. Example: `show manifest-G30-R5.0.0-F-2021.11.04_20_04-46.manifest`.

No. Versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type within one software-load. Use `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` or the shorter `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> of the SW load subcomponent, up to 64 characters. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive or installable. equipment-type is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use this firmware, 0..32 chars; fw-name and fw-version are also 0..32 chars. `show packaged-fw` lists all components' firmware versions in the load, for example packaged-fw-active/CHM6/DCO-OEC and packaged-fw-active/XMM4/IOP.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> ...` in Operational Mode, with option=validate to validate the software manifest/label and option=apply to apply it. Example: `prepare-upgrade validate <label>` then `prepare-upgrade apply <label>`. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. manifest is a leafref to a downloaded manifest-file. For unattended runs only, db-action selects empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db. clear-type (valid only for unattended with db-action empty-db) is full (default), keep-networking or initialize-from-script; keep-networking and initialize-from-script require new-admin-user (0..64 chars) and new-admin-password, and initialize-from-script requires script, a .cli file (default directory /storage/scripts).

`clear [-f] recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag. The action clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. Because of that reconfiguration it may be traffic impacting. The command runs in Operational Mode and has no parameters; the only flag is -f, which forces the command without confirmation. Use `clear recover-mode` to be prompted for confirmation, or `clear -f recover-mode` to skip the confirmation prompt.

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or, per equipment, `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. swload-state is active (active software load), inactive, or installable. Attributes include swload-version (0..64), swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false), both only relevant for the installable load, swload-status, swload-information (0..1024), swload-activation-type (direct = no reboot type determined, warmstart = warm reboot required, coldstart = cold reboot required, only relevant for installable), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-status values run status-unknown, validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed and timeout. Examples: `show software-load-active`, `show software-load-1-5/active`.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. location-id is the location of the equipment, a string of 0..64 characters, given as shelf-slot. For example, `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information from the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To drill into a specific load at that slot, use the sw-management form `show sw-management software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable]`, for example `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, or `show software-load-1-5/active` for the load attributes themselves.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply, both strings of 1...20 characters. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by this subtype, in gbps; max-capacity is the maximum capacity in gbps, where -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications lists the applications supported by this subtype and unsupported-applications lists those not supported, both of application type; if either list is empty, that constraint is not applicable. description is a string of 1...255 characters.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or the shorter `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name> ...`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The state attribute is the package state: installed (software package installed), not-installed (not installed), installation-failed (install failed) or unknown (state unknown); the default is unknown, so installation-failed is the value that flags a failed part of the load. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, 0..64 chars; swload-state is active, inactive or installable; name is the package name, 0..256 chars; version is 0..64 chars and description 0..512. Example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. `show sw-component` lists all components.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; `show sw-container` lists all OS-level containers with their attributes. cpu-usage is the container's current CPU usage in percentage, a number in the range 0...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. memory-usage is the current memory usage as a percentage, range 0...100%. state is off (default state, not launched yet), up (running) or exited. equipment is a leafref to the card AID the container runs on, and uptime is the time since the container started. Example: `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`. For per-service figures use `show sw-service-<sv-name>`.

Yes. `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>` creates a service-specific custom rule that overrides the default action on service failure; `set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>]` changes it, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]` displays it and `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>` removes it from the configuration. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. service-name is the name of the service to be monitored, a string 0..64 characters. fail-action values are default-action (restart the service, then reboot the system if the service does not recover), ignore (no automatic action taken on service failure) and system-restart (warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure). Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes: `show sw-management [downloads | software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] | software-load-active | software-load-inactive]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. It shows information about software locations, activity and downloads. `show sw-management downloads` lists the download history, that is the downloaded manifest files. `show sw-management software-load-active` shows the active software, including the sw-component-active/... packages, the packaged-fw-active/<equipment>/<fw-name> entries, and swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. `show sw-management software-load-inactive` shows the inactive load, and `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active` narrows it to one shelf-slot.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for all services and containers on the node. The reboot-count attribute is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16, and last-start-time is the time of the last service start/boot as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ; a high reboot-count with a recent last-start-time and a short uptime (reported in days:hours:minutes) indicates repeated restarting. state is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with state-details giving a brief description. sv-name is unique per service instance and contains card type, shelf and slot. Example: `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`.

`sw-component` reports at package level, keyed by <location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>. `sw-subcomponent` goes one level deeper, keyed by <location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>, so it shows the individual pieces inside a component. Syntax: `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]`, or without the location: `show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. sw-component-name and sw-subcomponent-name are strings 1..256. The same attributes are returned: state (installed, not-installed, installation-failed, unknown; default unknown), version (0..64) and description (0..512). Example: `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb`.

Run `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element, takes no parameters, and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output lists software-load-active, software-load-inactive and software-load-installable at NE level, each with its version and label, plus the same three states per location as software-load-<shelf>-<slot>/active, /inactive and /installable. For example: software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188, software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112, software-load-1-1/active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. file-status is the firmware file status with values valid, invalid or missing. crc is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, a string 0...64. path is the path for the firmware image, 0...255. applicable-eqpt is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to, and present-in-eqpt is the list of resources that already contain this version; both lists have max-elements 80. Also available are version, vendor and part-number (each 0...64) and nsa-upgrade-version, the versions from which the upgrade is non service affecting, 0...255.

Use `set transfer [http-proxy <value>]`, and `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]` to read it back; access mode is Operational and Candidate configuration. http-proxy is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of 0..1024 characters in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional; if <port> is omitted the default is 1080. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. transfer-progress is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100, default 0; bytes-transferred is the bytes transferred so far and total-bytes the total file size, both uint64 in bytes with default 0, and total-bytes stays zero until known at the transfer start. details is the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. operation is upload or download; last-completion-status may be success, fail, in-progress or unknown, where unknown occurs if the system rebooted mid-transfer. Transfer status exists only if at least one operation of that kind was done for the filetype. In synchronous mode a progress bar renders live in the CLI; asynchronous (-a) transfers are tracked here.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. It displays all SW versions being installed and their installation status, reported at NE level, chassis level and card level; resource (0..255 chars) specifies the object, and for ne and chassis the results are aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so compare the NE-level upgrade-partially-failed against the per-card entries to locate the failure. status values are idle (default), upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, apply-in-progress/-failed/-complete, activate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, cancel-in-progress/-complete/-failed and no-communication. step identifies the current upgrade step (0..128), with step-start-time; start-time and end-time show 'na' if idle or unfinished since startup, and details is 0..255.

Use `upload [-a] [-s] [filetype=]<value> ([destination=]<value> | [file-server=]<value> [[path=]<value>]) ...` in Operational mode with filetype=debug-log, which uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs. debug-entity is mandatory for debug-log and restricts the logs to a particular card/chassis; optional-content adds optional content. Example: `upload debug-log destination=scp://user@someserver//home/user`, producing debug_log_GX_11-18-11-2020-19.07.48.tar.gz. Certificates differ: for filetype local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate you must give certificate-name (1..128 chars), except for trusted-certificate where omitting it exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not, and output files are in P7 pem format. -a uploads asynchronously (track with `show transfer-status`), -s skips TLS/ssh known-host verification.

Run `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. ztp-state is the current state of the ZTP service, progressing through ztp-init (the default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, plus ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. ztp-completion-status summarizes completion on the node as not-completed (default) or completed. ztp-mode is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled with default enabled, set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when NBI is locked. ztp-details gives additional information on the current state, a string of 0..256 characters.

Use the capabilities command: `show capabilities-<name>`, where name is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the capability information for that card. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. There is no add/set/delete form; capabilities is read-only. For per-card-type capability data (node-type-compatibility, supported-subtype, supported-card-mode, card-width, max-power-draw, leds, console-port-support, support-serdes-config, supported-bands, supported-features) use `show supported-card-<card-type>`, for example `show supported-card-CHM1R`.

Provision with: `add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>`. Those three are mandatory. required-type is a String (length 0..32) drawn from the supported card list (CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, XMM4, UCM4, UTM2, SPN2, SPN2C, FAN, FAN-CTRL, PEM, BLANK, IOPANEL, OMD64, RD20TM and others). chassis-name is a String (length 1...255), default 1; slot-name is a String. Optional on add: required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name (settable only at (sub)card creation, e.g. 1-2.3), power-profile, alias-name, admin-state (lock/maintenance/unlock, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default Inhibited), label. Example: `add card-1-7 chassis-name 1 required-type CHM6 slot-name 7 required-subtype C6 power-profile low`.

On 1830 GX G40 a Native ZR TOM will not come up unless the chassis ambient temperature is configured. Set the chassis configured-ambient-temperature to 40C, for example `set chassis-1 configured-ambient-temperature 40`. If this parameter is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. configured-ambient-temperature is a number in Celsius units, has no default, and is used in add, set and show on the chassis object; it is the value used to compute the FRU power consumption. Verify with `show chassis-1 configured-ambient-temperature`, then re-provision the TOM.

Use `set console-<name> [baud-rate <value>]` and `show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state] [local-switch] [status]`. baud-rate accepts auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 or 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: in auto-sensing mode the system detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks it; the detected rate appears in actual-baud-rate and auto-sensing-state shows sensing or locked (default sensing, only visible when auto-sensing is enabled). Not all cards support auto-sensing. Example: `set console baud-rate 115200 local-switch force-enable`.

Use `show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]`. redundancy-status is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). redundancy-standby-status tells you readiness: ready-synchronized (standby is in sync and ready), not-ready-synchronizing (synchronizing data with the active controller, the default), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out) or card-not-present. additional-details is a string (0..128) with extra synchronization detail. number-of-switchover-events (uint32) and time-of-last-switchover are only visible on the active controller card. Example: `show controller-card-1-12`.

Use `show equipment [<option>]`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. With no option it lists the installed equipment of the node; supply an equipment option to narrow it to one item, for example `show equipment card-1-1`. The available options vary according to the installation. The per-card output lists the child objects (controller-card-1-1, console-1-1, port-1-1-AUX-1, port-1-1-CRAFT, port-1-1-DCN, port-1-1-U1) followed by the card attributes: required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label.

Both are controlled by equipment-policies: `set equipment-policies [tom-auto-migration <value>] [auto-assigned-directions <value>] [auto-assigned-degrees <value>] [cable-id-control <value>] [chassis-assignment-mode <value>] [comm-eth-location <value>]`. tom-auto-migration (enabled/disabled) enables automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; it may directly impact existing configuration, and it covers subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28). Degrees are not automatic by default: auto-assigned-degrees is enabled/disabled with default disabled, except enabled when l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. auto-assigned-directions is enabled by default. Example: `set equipment-policies tom-auto-migration enabled`.

You must enable it. SerDes templates are governed by the global flag use-serdes-templates on the equipment-templates object: `set equipment-templates [use-serdes-templates <value>]` and `show equipment-templates [use-serdes-templates]`. Values are enabled/disabled with default disabled (the CLI value completion offers false and true). On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively; they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact: the existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, whether it was applied via template or manually. Example: `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true`, then `show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates`.

Use the fru-info command: `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>`. It displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment type. manifest-file is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; equipment-type is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Neither has a default. The command is read-only and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For data about a FRU actually installed in the node (hardware-version, serial-number, clei, part-number, dates) use the inventory command instead.

Use the inventory command against the present FRU: `show inventory-<name> [serial-number] [clei] ...`, keyed by <card-name>-<port-name>, <card-name>.<slot-name>, <chassis-name>-<slot-name> or <name>. serial-number is the serial number of the equipment and clei is the Common Language Equipment Identifier, both Strings with no default. The same command also returns hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision (default 0), PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date and insertion-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ or 'NA'), number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code (0...18), actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw and fw-status. Examples: `show inventory` for everything, `show inventory-1-3-1` for a TOM.

Use `show led-<location>/<name> [status]` or `show leds`. location is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID), String length 1..32; name is the LED name within the FRU, String length 1..16. The status leaf reports: not-available (default), off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off (cycles all supported colors including off), cycling (cycles all supported colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. Yes, the LED object exists even if the FRU is not physically present; in that case status typically reads not-available. Example: `show led status` or `show leds led-1-1/active`.

Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted; use `show port-<card-name>-<port-name> [port-type] ...`. port-type values are: line (line-side 'colored' CWDM or DWDM module), tributary (standard 'grey' client interfaces), tributary-subport (a tributary split into subports), usb, comm, uplink (aggregation ports connecting to an adjunct line function), optical (general optical port, with or without monitoring), otdr (generic OTDR function, except external OTDR measurement), ocm and pluggable (the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM). In 1830 GX G40 there are three types of port: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports are on XMMs only, found on Slot 1 XMMs; trib/line ports appear on a CHM6 or CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7.

Use `show resources-<name> [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth]`, which also returns supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. The bandwidth leaves apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards. internal-cell-switch total and available default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. paired-slot total and available default to 500.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability, and to 0 if it does not. Example: `show resources-254-1` returns e.g. internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth 358.750 Gbit/s and paired-slot-available-bandwidth 258.750 Gbit/s.

Read the status leaf: `show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]`. status is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once it is configured, with values set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown, the default), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). Only status set confirms it took effect. You configure with `add serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> value <value>` or `set ... [value <value>]`, and remove with the delete form. A plain `show serdes` lists every parameter with its value and status, for example serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ 1 set.

A serdes-template is created per tom-part-number and applies to all line cards that support serdes; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is applied automatically. Syntax: `add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]`. tom-part-number is a string of length 1..16. ports-applicable narrows the ports: 'all' means all ports and is the default behavior, otherwise a string of length 1..16 per element with a maximum of 20 elements (completion offers T1 through T16 and all). Manual serdes configuration is still allowed and is kept even if it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Application depends on use-serdes-templates being set to 'true'; you can force re-application with the apply-template command.

Each individual parameter is a serdes-template-entry, composed of a serdes parameter name and its value: `add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>`. Edit with `set serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> [value <value>]`, remove with the delete form, and read with `show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]`. name is the name of the serdes parameter, string length 0....256; value is the value of the serdes parameter, string length 0...256; tom-part-number is string length 1..16. Examples: `add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3` and `set serdes-template-entry-TR-FC85S-NIN/TxEQ value 2`. Typical entry names are RxAmplitude, RxEQ, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor, TxEQ and TxEQAdaptive.

Yes. The serial-console object holds the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system and is managed by the system, so it cannot be manually deleted. Use `set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]` and `show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]`. global-switch allows access by serial console, with values enabled/disabled and default enabled; each console port can override this global behavior via the per-card console local-switch parameter (use-global-switch, force-enable, force-disable). global-timeout is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes with default 60; set it to zero to disable the inactivity timer. Example: `set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80`.

Use the slot command: `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]` (or `show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>` for a subslot). current-equipment is the name of the equipment currently required in that slot, for example 1-1, and shows --- when nothing is assigned. supported-type lists what can go there (for example CHM6,gx:UCM4) and installed-type shows what is physically installed, blank when no FRU is present. oper-state is enabled or disabled (default disabled) and avail-state carries values such as normal in-service or partially-faulted abnormal in-service. `show slot` lists every slot in the node; `show slot-1-1` shows a single slot.

Use `show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]`. card-name is the name of the card supporting the sub-component, string length 0..64; sub-component-name is the name of the sub-component; AID is the Resource Access Identifier, string length 1..64; description is a user configurable description of the sub-component, string length 0..128. Running `show sub-component` with no key lists them all, for example sub-component-1-6/dco-oec with AID 1-6-dco-oec and description 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component'. To see which sub-components a card has, `show resources-<name> supported-sub-components` lists the sub-components present in the card that can be addressed for operations such as restart.

Use `show supported-card-<card-type> [node-type-compatibility] ...`, for example `show supported-card-CHM1R`. node-type-compatibility is the supported NE node-type for a sled card and takes the values all (compatible with any node-type), ILA (In-Line Amplifier, two-directions) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer). It is only of relevance for line-card(s) and carrier-card(s). The same command also returns supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw in Watts, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features. `show supported-card` lists all card types.

Use `show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> [controller-redundancy-supported] [number-of-front-slots] [number-of-rear-slots] ...`, for example `show supported-chassis-G31`. controller-redundancy-supported is true or false and states whether that chassis type supports controller redundancy. number-of-front-slots and number-of-rear-slots are uint8 counts of the equipment holder slots on the front and back plates. The command also returns supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, power-control-supported, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (not-applicable, optional-dust-filter, dust-filter-regularly-replaced; default optional-dust-filter), depth in mm, height in RUs, leds, supported-subchassis-type (maximum 10 elements, empty means no multi-chassis) and supported-features. Example output: supported-chassis-G42, redundancy true, 7 front slots, 12 rear slots, 600 mm, 3 RU.

Use `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> [port-type] [direction] [configuration-mode] [faceplate-label] [leds] [present] [default-tom] [parent-port] [subport-list] [allows-auto-migration]`, for example `show supported-port-CHM1R/2`. port-type says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, ocm or pluggable. configuration-mode says who provisions it: system-configured (the system configures it automatically and the user cannot make changes) or user-configured (the user can provision or de-provision). faceplate-label identifies the port on the card faceplate (1..36 chars), present is always or in-node-controller-only (default always), default-tom names the TOM present by default, and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true) indicates whether TOMs on this port type are auto migrated per the equipment-policies tom-auto-migration flag.

Use `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> [possible-card-types] [requires-blank-when-empty] ...` (a <card-type>/<slot-name> form exists for subslots). requires-blank-when-empty states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty, with values not-applicable, optional and required. On a G42, slots 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and PEM-1 to PEM-4 are required, while slot 2, the FAN slots and FANCTRL-1 are not-applicable. possible-card-types lists the card types allowed in that slot, maximum 15 elements (for example XMM4 in slot 1, CHM6,UCM4 in slots 4-7). The command also returns slot-location (front/rear), slot-vertical-position and slot-horizontal-position, configuration-mode (system-configured or user-configured), auto-provision-capable, default-card, reset-power in W at 55C, virtual-slot (default false) and leds (maximum 10).

Use `show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]`. It reports the TOM capabilities in the scope of a particular card and port. tom-type is the form factor (CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD and so on) and tom-subtype-group is a string of length 0..32 such as '4x100GE-breakout'. supported-phy-mode lists the phy-modes supported in that TOM on that card, drawn from 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G; default-phy-mode is the one used by default, from the same value set. Examples: `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28` and `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout`.

Use `show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]`. supported-power-class is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, uint8 in the range 1..8; the port may only partially support that class, so read supported-max-power-draw, a decimal64 giving the maximum power in watts the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class. tom-type is the pluggable form factor identity matching the TOM required-type (CFP2-DCO, QSFPDD, QSFP28 and so on). To see what the fitted module actually reports, `show inventory-... actual-power-class actual-max-power-draw`; those are populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules, not for native qualified subtypes.

Yes. The Tributary Port termination point is auto-created when the TOM is created, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. You provision with add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>, where required-type is mandatory and takes CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP or SFPPLUS. Optional attributes on add/set are required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name (0..256), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label (0..256), enable-serdes (false/true, default false) and power-mode (not-powered/powered, default powered; CHM7 cards only). card-name and port-name are strings 0..64. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD.

Use show tom-type-<tom-type> support-third-party-toms. The support-third-party-toms attribute is a boolean (false, true) stating whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to supported Nokia TOMs. The same show also returns description (string 0..255), tom-type (identityref), data-rate (uint16, Gbps) and generic-subtype (the 3rd party subtype string for this TOM). Run show tom-type with no key to list all types. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode; tom-type is show-only. When you do install a third-party module, the tom command carries power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), which is used to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It shows up under unprovisioned-inventory, which lists detected inventory that has not yet been accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. Use show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>. chassis-serial-number is the residing chassis serial number (string 0..16) and slot-name is the residing slot name (string 0..16); if the equipment is the chassis itself, slot-name is empty. Retrievable attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ) and detection-timestamp, which is the last time the Node Controller detected the unprovisioned equipment. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted, a string of length 0..32, and it can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations. available-space is the current free storage and total-space is the total storage in the file-system, both uint16 in MB. All three (available-space, total-space, usb-path) apply only if type is storage; the other type value is power-supply, for powering external equipment such as passive shelves. present indicates the presence state of the USB connector (true, false; default false). Example for one port: show usb-1-5-U1. Run show usb with no key to list every USB port on the node with its type and present state.

Use activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]. db-instance names the database snapshot to be activated and defaults to temp. The paraphrase is a short description of the database to be activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override is the action to override the sanity check, values true or false, default false. Access is Operational mode. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken before you can activate it, using take-snapshot. Existing snapshots can be listed with show database. Example: activate-snapshot onehour, or activate-snapshot sanity-check-override.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after enable-advanced-parameters on the optical carrier is set to true. Separately, if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, running show advanced-parameter reports 'ERROR: object does not exist' - that is the error you are seeing. Also note that if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value the configuration is not rejected; show advanced-parameter then reports the failed status for that parameter. The status attribute takes failed, in-progress, not-supported, set or unknown, with default unknown. Syntax: add advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Use apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*]). The template-type value serdes-template applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in the applicable-tom parameter. applicable-tom is the list of TOMs to apply the serdes-templates against; if it is not provided (the list is empty), all system TOMs are considered for template application. The guide lists the template-type default as serdes-templage. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: apply-template serdes-template, or apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1; command completion offers the eligible applicable-tom values such as tom-1-7-T1 through tom-1-7-T15.

Yes, use commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a 'persist' trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. You confirm with commit persist and abandon with commit cancel. A Persistent Confirmed Commit requires the commands to carry an -id parameter, which is the ID shared by the commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel commands. All of these must be done in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with the configure command. commit -m=<message> attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use show config | display commands and store the result for later usage; the guide names this as the good way to create a CLI script that restores the system configuration. show config displays the system's configuration, skipping configurations that have their default values, and is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. You can narrow it with show config <entity-id> for one instance or show config <entity-type> for all entities of a type. The display piped command's commands mode displays the configurations as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, which is what makes the output replayable; show -r | display commands produces a CLI script from all system configurations.

That depends on the target you pick. configure <target> takes exclusive, where only this session can make changes to the candidate configuration, or shared, where multiple sessions can make changes to the candidate configuration. The default target is exclusive. The command moves you from operational mode into Candidate Configuration mode, and its access mode is Operational mode. It also sets the candidate starting point: by default a copy of the Running Datastore; from-default gives a blank config; from-script=<script> imports CLI commands from a text file; from-commit=<commit-id> initializes from a past commit, available only when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive.

Use show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]. This command shows the current values of the advanced parameters that are running on the system, as opposed to the configured values returned by show advanced-parameter. optical-carrier-name is the name of the optical carrier supporting the advanced parameter and current-advanced-parameter-name is the parameter name, both strings; value is the value running on the system, a string. Run show current-advanced-parameter for all of them, or scope it to one carrier, for example show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*. Typical output lists entries such as BOASetting, CRAvgNCtrl, ClockPreEmphasis, EEPNNLMitigation, NLC, RxCDCompCtrl and TxSignalBWControl, and the running value can differ from the configured one. PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified. Access mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

No. clear database performs a full wipe of database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity. It does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data; use the clear system command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Syntax: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>; -f forces without confirmation. clear-type takes full (default, factory defaults), keep-networking (wipe but keep network configuration) or initialize-from-script (wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script, default directory /storage/scripts). The latter two require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Transient alarms after the controller reboot can be ignored.

Use db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>. The type parameter defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption; encryption-with-integrity is the one that adds the integrity protection on top of encryption. -f forces the command without confirmation. Access mode is Operational Mode. Running db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity enables the integrity check for the system database and will automatically reboot the controller. Afterwards verify with show db-protection-scheme, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and states that it can be changed via the db-migrate RPC; integrity-algorithm will then show hmac-sha2-512 instead of none.

Use show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode] and read integrity-status, which indicates the status of the integrity check with values passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup or disabled. The other attributes are encryption-algorithm, whose value is xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size); integrity-algorithm, either hmac-sha2-512 or none; and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. On a node that has not been migrated the output reads integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled, mode encryption-only.

Use diff [-t|-c] candidate, which must be run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists created, deleted or changed objects between the candidate datastore and the current system configuration, showing only configurable attributes; 'new' data is the candidate and 'old' data is the current system configuration. Output forms: normal diff style, where + is added objects or new values and - is deleted objects or old values; side-by-side with the -t flag; CLI commands reproducing the candidate changes with the -c flag, which is the form you want; and the list of commands being executed with -d. diff commit <id> [<id>] compares a commit-record against the running configuration or another commit-record, and is only displayed when commit-records exist, that is when commit-tracking is enabled in system-policies, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Use discard-changes. It discards all candidate datastore content and the CLI returns to operational mode, so nothing you staged is committed and the running configuration is untouched. The command takes no parameters and no flags; the syntax is simply discard-changes. Its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode, so you must already be in the candidate session entered with the configure command. If instead you want to keep the session but revert to an earlier committed state, that is the rollback commit command, not discard-changes.
