An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that you enable by name: add extended-config-<name>, delete extended-config-<name>, show extended-config-<name> [description]. Treat it carefully, because it introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, and it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side; the name you give must match a name already known by the system. name is a string of length 0..64. The description attribute is provided by the system and displays the description of the extended-config and its effect in the system (string 0..255), so read it before adding one. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Check the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> and read service-impact, which identifies whether applying this parameter change causes service impact; values are service-affecting or non-service-affecting. If it is service-affecting, you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations, before applying it. configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change, with values no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change and full-config-no-pll-change. The same show also returns description, type, supported-values (a list of ranges or discrete numbers), direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity (uint8, how many values you must enter). All attributes are read-only. Example: show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/*.

Use lock, which locks database access to the current session and grants exclusive write access to that CLI session. It is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, another session, CLI or any other type, that tries to make a configuration will receive an error. A lock will not be possible if another session is currently holding the lock. The lock is released in two ways: by using the unlock command, or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether the user closes it explicitly, an administrator closes the session, or it drops on inactivity time-out. Syntax is lock [-h], where -h displays help; there are no other parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode.

A named-value-set is addressed by two keys, the database entry name and the set name, in the form named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>. db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for this named-value-set. It holds a single value attribute, a string of length 1..1024 characters. Supported commands are add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>], set with the same form, show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value], and delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

That is controlled by recovery restore-from-chassis-storage, set with set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value> and read with show recovery. Values are disabled (chassis storage is not used for restoration in this NE), auto-restore (SW and DB are stored on chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, then a manual clear recovery-mode is needed, letting you validate the restored system before affecting the HW), and auto-in-service (same restore, but on success the NC automatically leaves recovery mode). The default is auto-in-service, so by default the replacement does pick the configuration up on its own. show recovery also returns restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore; default init), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup.

Only if the candidate is empty. rollback must be executed with the commit parameter and optionally a specific commit-id: rollback commit [<commit-id>]. If no commit-id is provided, the most recent commit-record is used. The command works both in the Running Datastore, which is the default, and in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty; that is in fact a way to initialize the Candidate. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

show commit retrieves commit record information, letting you visualize the Commit Repository records, but it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither is true on your node you get nothing back. Turn it on with set system-policies commit-tracking enabled; commit-tracking defaults to disabled, and disabling it clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. Syntax is show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>], where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -n selects an exact number of records to obtain, and -s takes a timestamp and shows all records created since it. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use set system-policies [commit-tracking <value>] [writable-running <value>] and read them back with show system-policies. commit-tracking enables the commit-repository feature; with it enabled, all configuration changes done via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records, which can then be visualized, compared and rolled back. Values are enabled or disabled, default disabled; disabling clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. writable-running also takes enabled or disabled with default disabled; disabling writable-running makes configure commands via the running datastore impossible, so the candidate datastore becomes mandatory: CLI add/set/delete only in Candidate mode, NETCONF edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, and RESTCONF, gNMI (telemetry still allowed, gNOI still allowed), the WebGUI and TL1 all become read-only. Access mode: Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode.

The db-passphrase is missing. The system will only accept take-snapshot if the db-passphrase, used for DB snapshot encryption, is configured, either in global configuration as part of the security-policies via set security-policies db-passphrase, or locally as a parameter of the command, take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. The passphrase requires a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and special characters are allowed in accordance with the 85-character set known as Z85. Automatic DB snapshots will not be enabled until this parameter is set. Syntax: take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]. db-instance takes temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is a string 0..128. Access mode is Operational Mode. List existing snapshots with show database.

Use a template entry. A template is a single rule defined by an object/attribute pair plus the value to use as that attribute's default. Syntax: add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. object is the object name (e.g. odu), attribute the attribute name (e.g. admin-state), and value the value to apply (e.g. lock) and is mandatory. sequence-id is a number in range 1..65535 that defines processing order, lower ids first. condition is optional and restricts the rule (e.g. service-type=OTU4); label is an optional free string. Example: add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

No. A template-group is a configuration group holding a list of template entries, created with add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>], and shown or removed with show template-group-<name> and delete template-group-<name>. The enabled attribute takes true or false, and its default is true only if there is no other template-group already enabled. So the first group you add comes up enabled by itself (add template-group-1), but a second group will not default to enabled while another one is active. name and label are strings. The commands run in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show templates. This command displays the configuration that defines the data model for system templates, i.e. the overall templates container on the node. It takes no parameters, and the whole syntax is simply: show templates. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the level below it, use show template-group-<name> to see an individual configuration group (with enabled and label), and show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> to see an individual template entry (sequence-id, object, attribute, value, label, condition).

No. The unlock command releases a database previously locked with the lock command, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a database that was locked by another session, or a database that is not locked at all, the unlock command fails. There is a way out without their help: a lock is automatically released if the session that took the lock is closed, so once that operator's session ends the database frees up. After the unlock, any session can perform configurations and can take a new lock. Syntax is unlock [-h], where -h displays help; it runs in Operational Mode.

Yes, use validate. It validates the contents of a specified configuration, covering any CLI command used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging or replacing content, without committing it. Syntax: validate candidate <candidate> command <string>. The candidate parameter is the candidate datastore targeted for validation, and command is the command text to validate, both strings with no default. If the command validates, the reply is OK; otherwise the command fails. Multiple CLI commands can be supplied in one call if separated with a semicolon. Example: validate 'set ne altitude 600'. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

A maximum of 7 rounds of additional-key-exchange can be configured, with additional-key-exchange-id in range 1..7, and each round must use a unique key-exchange algorithm. The rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Syntax: add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>. dh-group values are dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. Configuring it is optional, it brings the IKE session down immediately to renegotiate, and the Child SA key exchange is derived from IKE. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm; ml-kem-1024 is recommended as strongest.

Use show data-path-encryption. That is the complete syntax; the command shows the datapath encryption attributes and takes no parameters. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related objects for L1 encryption detail are secure-entity, secure-entity-sa-proposal and secure-application, and the global L1 policy that decides whether the NE validates the certificate subject alternate name against the IKE ID is set with set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <match|ignore>.

Use the encryption-algorithm command, where both the algorithm and key length are part of the AID. Syntax: add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>, and there is also a form without ipsec-spd-entry-name for the IKE SA level; show and delete take the same paths. algorithm values are null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16 and chacha20-poly1305. key-length values are none, key-length-128, key-length-192 and key-length-256, with none as the default. number is the proposal number, range 1..max. Example: add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

With ike-sa-proposal, integrity-algorithm and dh-group are mandatory on add; prf is optional. Syntax: add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number> integrity-algorithm <value> dh-group <value> [prf <value>]. number is the proposal number, range 1..max. integrity-algorithm values: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf values: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. protocol-id is read-only and always IKE. Example: add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192.

The top-level ikev2 object carries a single attribute, data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy that indicates whether the NE must validate the certificate Subject Alternative Name against the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore, with no stated default. Syntax: set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>] and show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]. Example: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Read host-card-encryption-capability on the ikev2-local-instance: it indicates whether the card on which the IKEv2 local instance runs supports encryption, with values yes, no and unknown, default unknown, and it is show-only. The address is governed by local-address-assignment-method, a show-only attribute with values auto and manual, default auto; local-address is the local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, default 0.0.0.0, and it is settable. Syntax: set ikev2-local-instance-<name> [scope <value>] [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [local-address <value>]. scope values are data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method. admin-state is lock, maintenance, unlock (default unlock); oper-state enabled/disabled (default disabled); alarm-report-control allowed/inhibited (default inhibited). host-card references the service card. Example: set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132.

On ikev2-peer, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. re-auth-frequency is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200. The rule is that re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency must not be multiples of each other, and they must differ by a few minutes so there is a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Related failure handling: re-key-fail-policy takes kill traffic or continue traffic, default continue-traffic, and re-key-traffic-kill-offset is 0..86400 seconds, default 0; re-auth-traffic-kill-offset is likewise 0..86400 seconds, default 0, being the wait before killing all Child SAs tied to the IKE SA. Set them with set ikev2-peer-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name> [re-key-frequency <value>] [re-auth-frequency <value>].

Use ipsec-sa-proposal. On add, dh-group is mandatory and integrity-algorithm is optional: add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]. dh-group values are dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm values are none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. Two attributes are show-only and fixed: protocol-id is ESP (default ESP) and esn is esn (default esn). number is the proposal number, range 1..max. Example: add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256.

Yes. The ipsec-sa-re-key object supports time-based and volume-based re-keying: add ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> [frequency <value>] [bytes <value>] [packets <value>], with matching set, show and delete. frequency is the re-keying frequency for the IPsec child SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. bytes re-keys on the amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. packets re-keys on the amount of packets transmitted, either disabled or a number in range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The action attribute of ipsec-spd-entry indicates the IPsec treatment given to matching IP datagrams, with values protect, bypass and discard, default protect. Tunnelling is separate: the mode attribute selects transport or tunnel, and its default is tunnel, so yes, by default a protected entry tunnels. Syntax: add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <value> [description <value>] [action <value>] [ipsec-protocol <value>] [mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [esn <value>] [anti-replay-window <value>] [dynamic-ts <value>]. priority is a uint8 and is mandatory, giving precedence between entries. ipsec-protocol is ESP (default ESP). esn is true/false, default true. anti-replay-window applies when action = protect, range 32..1024, default 64. dynamic-ts is disabled/enabled, default disabled. alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

Create an ipsec-traffic-selector under the SPD entry, then attach address and port ranges to it. Syntax: add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]. next-layer-protocol is the inner (upper layer) protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol field or the IPv6 next header field; values are any (value 0), opaque (value 255) or a number in range 0-255, default any. ipsec-traffic-selector-name is a string of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). The actual addresses and ports come from the child objects local-subnet, remote-subnet, local-ports and remote-ports keyed on this selector. Example: add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17.

Because start and stop are part of the AID, not settable attributes. The local-ports command only offers add, show and delete: add local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, plus show and delete on the same path. There is no set form, so to change a range you delete the old entry and add a new one. start takes all, opaque or a port number. stop is a port-number and defaults to 0 if not supplied; the value 0 is only accepted when start is set to all or opaque. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all, and for a single port add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53.

Add a local-subnet under the traffic selector. Syntax: add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>, with show and delete on the same path. There is no set form, so the prefix is part of the AID and changing it means delete then add. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, and broadcast for IPv4 only). ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32; the local instance, peer and traffic selector names are strings of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Example: add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

That depends on link-security-control on the macsec-entity, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. Its values are must-secure and should-secure, and the default is must-secure, so out of the box unsecured traffic is not passed. Syntax: add macsec-entity-<name> [supporting-facility <value>] [enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [link-security-control <value>] [replay-protection <value>] [replay-protection-window <value>], with set, show and delete forms. enabled is true/false, default true; alarm-report-control is allowed/inhibited, default inhibited; replay-protection is enable/disable; replay-protection-window is the number of packets in range 0..4294967295, default 0. Example: add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3.

Set the pre-shared key on the macsec-mka object: set macsec-mka-<name> [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [mka-policy <value>] [connectivity-association-key <value>] [connectivity-association-key-name <value>] [psk-lifetime <value>] [psk-expiration-warning <value>] [psk-lifetime-enable <value>]. connectivity-association-key is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and connectivity-association-key-name its name, both strings of length 0..64. To find the key server, read is-key-server, which identifies whether the local end is key server; values true and false, default false. Also shown are psk-configured-timestamp, psk-lifetime and psk-expiration-warning (range 1..173 days, 14 days) and psk-lifetime-enable (enabled/disabled). Example: set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa.

On the mka-policy, the MKA policy referenced by the macsec entity for an Ethernet facility. Syntax: add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>], with set, show and delete forms. macsec-cipher-suite selects the cipher suite for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation, listed with values true and false and default true. sak-rekey-interval is the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0|30..65535, default 30s. key-server-priority is the priority the MKA protocol uses to select the key server. confidentiality-offset specifies the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain-text, listed with values allowed and inhibited, default inhibited. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the re-auth command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>, where ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (the IKE SA), given as a string. Access Mode is Operational mode only. Both forms of the reference work, for example re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202 and re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2. For the scheduled equivalent, set re-auth-frequency on the ikev2-peer (3600..604800 seconds, default 43200).

The re-key command performs on-demand re-keying against one of three targets: a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec Child security association (a Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>. ipsec-security-association points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), ikev2-peer references the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and secure-entity points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all three are strings. Access Mode is Operational mode. Examples: re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1 and re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX.

Set the start value to all and leave the stop value off. The remote-ports syntax is add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, with show and delete on the same path and no set form. start takes all, opaque or a port number. stop is a port-number and defaults to 0 when it is not set; the value 0 is only accepted by the system if start is all or opaque, which is what makes the bare all form legal. Examples: add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all for every port, and add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49 for a single port.

Add a remote-subnet under the traffic selector of the SPD entry: add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>. show and delete use the same path; there is no set form, so the prefix is part of the key and a change means delete then add. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, and broadcast for IPv4 only). ipsec-spd-entry-name is a string of length 1..32; the instance, peer and traffic selector names are strings of length 1..64 matching pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). Example: add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the sc-rx (Receiving Secure Channel) show command: show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. The state attribute is the one that tells you whether the channel is carrying traffic; it is returned by the MKA stack and has two values: in-use, meaning Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use, and not-in-use, meaning no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use. The key is name (string, length 0..64) plus index, the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-rx is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

sc-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel object and it is read-only: the only form is show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]. There is no add, set or delete for sc-tx, so you cannot configure it. It is keyed by name (string, length 0..64) and index, the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). sci-tx is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. state is reported by the MKA stack as in-use (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use) or not-in-use (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign the certificate with set secure-application-<id> active-certificate-id <value>, for example set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client; multiple certificates are given as a comma list, for example set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY. id is a string of length 0..20 and active-certificate-id a string of length 0..128. show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert] reports which one is actually in-use (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id), the type (server or client) and status (enabled or disabled); show secure-applications lists them all. To demand a client certificate, set verify-client-cert, which enables TLS Mutual Authentication: disabled (default) means no client certificate is requested, required means the client certificate is required and validated. Changes take effect only for new TLS connections.

That depends on re-key-fail-policy on the secure entity. It indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful, and takes kill-traffic or continue-traffic, defaulting to continue-traffic, so by default traffic is not dropped. If you set kill-traffic, traffic-kill-offset gives the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. Both are settable with add secure-entity-<name> ... or set secure-entity-<name> [re-key-frequency <value>] [re-key-fail-policy <value>] [traffic-kill-offset <value>]. Related, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer, 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800. Example: add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is a show-only object with a single fixed proposal: show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]. There is no add or set form. Every attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: number is 1, encryption-algorithm is aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length is key-length-256, integrity-algorithm is none, and dh-group is ecp-521. The integrity-algorithm and dh-group are the values advertised to the far-end secure entity peer. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. What you can tune on the encryption entity itself is the secure-entity re-key behaviour, not the algorithm suite.

Through the security-policy-database (SPD), which is keyed by the local IKE instance and the peer and carries the secure entity as an attribute: add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]. ikev2-local-instance is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance and ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (the IKE SA); both are strings. associated-secure-entity is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). You can also use set to change it, show security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity] to read it, and delete security-policy-database-<...> to remove the entry. Example on 1830 GX G40: add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with a manually configured CRL Distribution Point. Each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Configure it with add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>], and adjust later with set cdp-<name> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]. url is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. enabled (true, false, default false) enables automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or update is performed but existing CRLs are unaffected. refresh-interval is either the special enum use-next-update, which takes the next refresh time from the current CRL next-update field, or a duration written as [xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs], for example 2w, 5d 12h, or 1h 7m 30s. show cdp-<name> also reports next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result; show cdps lists all. Requires System Administrator privilege.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate: cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]. days is the number of days the certificate is valid for and defaults to 365. certificate-name is a string of length 1..128, org-name a string 1..64, common-name the IP or host name that identifies the server (1..64), and subject the full certificate subject name (1..1024); when generating a self-signed certificate you must specify either subject or common-name. auto-install (true, false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application that has no active certificate. -f forces the command without confirmation. The command runs in Operational mode. Example: cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true.

Through cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules mapping an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity. Each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly. Create one with add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]. map-type is extract or map. field applies only when map-type is extract and names the certificate attribute used to determine identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn, san-uri. mapped-user-name is required only when map-type is map and gives the local or remote user identity. criteria defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked, priority ranges 1 to 255, and issuer (value any) restricts the rule to certificates from a specific issuer in the trust chain. enabled defaults to True. Example: add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name.

Delete it with clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>, which removes already imported local, trusted or peer X509v3 certificates. type is trusted, local or peer, and id is the certificate ID (string, length 0..128) which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to get the list of certificate-ids that can be cleared. type also accepts the bulk options purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. Without -f you are prompted Are you sure? [y/n]. Examples: clear certificate local certX, clear certificate type=trusted id=certY, clear certificate trusted id=root. To see what is installed, run show certificates, which displays all managed local, trusted and peer X509v3 certificates imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; show certificate-revocation shows certificate revocations. Access is Operational mode.

Use the clear crl command with a clear-target rather than naming each CRL: clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>. The targets are single-crl (the default, which removes only the CRL named in <crl-name>, which is then mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), purge-invalid-crls (purge all invalid CRLs), purge-cached-crls (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or a certificate CDP extension), and purge-all-crls (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale ones, use clear crl purge-invalid-crls; use <tab> to list clearable CRL names. -f forces without confirmation. Check first with show crls or show crl-<name>, where status is valid, expired or future and type is cached or manually. Example: clear crl single-crl myCA-1. Clear runs in Operational mode; show is also available in Candidate Configuration mode.

csr-gen creates a local-certificate in the pending-import state and outputs a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then signed by an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded back into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. Until that download happens, show local-certificate-<id> reports status pending-import, meaning the certificate was generated by CSR but import is not yet complete. Syntax: csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...]. key-algorithm defaults to eccp256; signature-hash-algorithm defaults to sha256 for rsa2048, rsa3072 and eccp256, sha384 for eccp384, sha512 for rsa4096 and eccp521. metadata-template defaults to generic. The subject CN RDN is mandatory. Runs in Operational mode. Example: csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia'.

Use display-cert with the display-type parameter: display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>. display-type defines the requested type of display operation and accepts all-certificate-hierarchy, certificate-details and certificate-hierarchy, with all-certificate-hierarchy as the default. So chain views are what you get by default; pass display-type=certificate-details when you want only that certificate's own fields. The certificate parameter is the certificate to display, given by its full name such as trusted-certificate-ca_root, local-certificate-server_cert or local-certificate-pace_client; pressing <tab> at certificate= lists the available names. The command also displays CSR details. Output includes version, serial number, signature algorithm, issuer, validity Not Before / Not After, subject, public key info and X509v3 extensions. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS and replaces the complex manual CSR process; the device includes an EST client that talks to a dedicated EST server. Syntax: est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] [metadata-from-certificate=]<value> [metadata-from-cnf=]<value> [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>] [[key-usage=]...] [[extended-key-usage=]...] [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]. target-command is cacerts, enroll or re-enroll. est-ca defaults to 1. key-algorithm accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; signature-hash-algorithm is sha512, sha384 or sha256, default sha256; metadata-template defaults to generic. Example: est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>.

Yes, via est-ca: set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>], read back with show est-ca-<name>. auto-re-enrollment specifies how far before expiration re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA. It takes a number of days before expiration from 1 to 365, or a percentage of the not-after minus not-before interval rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%, or disabled. The default is Disabled, so automatic re-enrollment is off until you configure it. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example through expiration. The CA is pinned by explicit-ca-root, the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, and root-fingerprint, which verifies the Root CA identity using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to secure the initial connection. Example: set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40.

The EST server port is set by server-port and defaults to 443. Configure servers with add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>], and change them with set est-server-<name>/<server-name> [...] or remove them with delete est-server-<name>/<server-name>. Yes, you can define more than one: priority defines the server's precedence with a value range of 1 to 10, and if omitted the priority defaults to the current lowest precedence (the highest existing number) plus one; if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. server-address is the IP address of the EST server. enabled is True or False, defaulting to True. path-segment is an optional label added to the EST base url, a string of length 0..64. Example: add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE: import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. certificate-name is the name the certificate will be known by in the system. passphrase decodes encrypted input certificates and applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles. The -i flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for a single certificate it imports intermediates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example issuer /CN=Nokia yields trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, trusted-certificate-Nokia-2. import-certificate -h displays help. Runs in Operational mode. Example: import-certificate peer-certificate certificate-name=peer-cert1 <string in PEM format>.

Check the ISK attributes before clearing. show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time], or show ISKs for the list. is-key-in-use indicates if the key is in use in this FRU (true, false, default false), is-key-verified indicates if the key is verified in this FRU (true, false, default false), and being-deleted is set to true once the system receives an ISK delete command, indicating deletion is in progress and the ISK will soon be removed. KRK-name names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one, use clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>, where the name of the key to be deleted must be provided; key-name is a string of length 0..64 and -f forces without confirmation. Example: show ISK-1-5-0-ISK_E1, then clear isk key-name=name.

Use show KRKs to list all Image Root Keys on the system, and show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] for a single one. KRK is read-only; there is no add, set or clear form. name is the unique representation of the object, CPU is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0 (uint8), key-name is the key name (string, length 0..64), key-serial-number is the Key Serial Number, issuer-name is the name of the CSA, or Code Signing Appliance (string, length 0..20), key-length is the key length in bits (uint16), and key-payload is the key payload in hex format (string, length 0..1100). Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1.

Use show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]. It is show-only. install-status indicates whether this KRP has been installed in the system and takes not-installed, installing, installed or failed. KRP-version is the package version, issuer-name is the name of the CSA, or Code Signing Appliance (string, length 0..20), and KRK-name is the name of the KRK, the Image Root Key, that signed this ISK. signature-hash-scheme is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512, signature-algorithm is ECDSA, RSA or none, signature-payload is a hex string of 0..1024, and signature-gen-time is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the revocation-mode attribute on the local certificate: set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]. revocation-mode controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined and takes auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, with auto as the default. Setting force-revoked makes the node treat the certificate as revoked regardless of CRL or OCSP results; force-unrevoked does the opposite. The id is a string of length 1..128 matching the pattern ([A-Za-z0-9_.,/@][A-Za-z0-9_-.,/@]*). Read it back with show local-certificate-<id> [...] [status] [revocation-mode] [used-by] [...]; status reports revoked among values such as valid, expired, untrusted, future and pending-import, and used-by lists the secure-applications, ikev2-peers and other objects presently using the certificate. The same revocation-mode attribute with the same values and default exists on peer-certificate. Access is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Add it with add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>], then adjust with set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] or remove it with delete ocsp-server-<name>. priority sorts the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, and the range is uint8 1..10, so priority 1 is tried first. name is a string of length 0..64. url is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form http://<host>[:<port>], where host may be an IPv4 or IPv6 address or a DNS name, and if the port is omitted the default HTTP port 80 is used; the string is 0..1024 with pattern http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*). enabled controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status, true or false, default false. show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query] also reports last-query, the timestamp of the last successful query. Example: add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application. Its white-listed attribute is read-only and takes true or false, defaulting to false. If true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain, listed in trust-chain as a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. View it with show peer-certificate[-id] [version] [serial-number] [subject-name] [issuer] [trust-chain] [valid-from] [valid-to] [status] [...] [white-listed] [alarm-report-control] [label] [...]. What you can change is set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]: revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked with default auto, and alarm-report-control is inhibited or allowed with default allowed. status values include valid, revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future and unsupported.

SSH direct shell access listens on port 8022 by default and is off by default. Both are attributes of the ssh object: set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>], read back with show ssh [enabled] [port] [pre-login-message] [post-login-message]. enabled enables direct access to shell via ssh and takes true or false, defaulting to false. port is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell, a number in the range 1..65535, default 8022. pre-login-message is the welcome message displayed before user login, a string of length 0..1440, with no default. post-login-message is displayed after user login, also 0..1440, and defaults to a Warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Use add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]; change the label with set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>], view it with show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label], and remove it with delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>, which prompts for confirmation. user-name is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user (string 0..32); key-id is a unique identifier for the entry (string 1..64). public-key is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) public key component encoded in PEM format as <key type><SPACE>base64 encoded OpenSSH public key<SPACE><comment>, up to 2048 characters. public-key-algorithm is read-only and reports ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNhLXNoYTIt...

The node's global SSHv2 host keys (used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 based apps) are shown with 'show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm> [public-key] [label] [fingerprint-algorithm] [fingerprint]'. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, there is more than one. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. Supported public-key-algorithm values: ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts at R9.0). public-key is PEM encoded, String 0..2048 characters; label is String 0..256; fingerprint-algorithm is md5 or sha256; fingerprint is String 0..95. Access mode: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: 'show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521'.

ssh-keygen generates a private/public key pair and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. Syntax: 'ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]', Operational mode only. -t is rsa, ecdsa or ed25519, default rsa. Key lengths with secure mode disabled: RSA 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048), ECDSA 256, 384 or 521 (default 256). With secure mode enabled (check security-policies/secure-mode): RSA only 4096, ECDSA 384 or 521 (default 384). ED25519 supports 256 irrespective of secure mode, and is available starting R9.0. -l=<key-label> is the label associated with the key; if no value is provided the label is the value of ne-id. Retrieve the resulting public key with 'show ssh-host-key'.

Pre-trust an outbound SSH peer with an ssh-known-host entry: 'add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]'. id is a unique name, String 0..64 characters. address is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host, and may carry a zone index after a % sign (numeric canonical form; default zone used if absent). public-key-algorithm is one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 from R9.0). public-key is the OpenSSH host public key in PEM format, String 0..2048 characters. label is String 0..256. 'set ssh-known-host-<id>' can only change label; 'show' and 'delete ssh-known-host-<id>' also exist. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

The trusted-certificate object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Commands: 'set trusted-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show trusted-certificate[-id]' with read-only attributes version (v3), serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, modification-time, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/rsa3072/rsa4096/ecdsa256/ecdsa384/ecdsa521), public-key-type (rsa, ecdsa), signature-key-type (rsa, ecdsa, rsassa-pss), signature-hash-algorithm (sha256, sha384, sha512, sha1), certificate-bytes, key-usage and extended-key-usage. revocation-mode is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto. alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default allowed. To remove a certificate use the 'clear certificate' command. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Stop it with 'terminate cable-id' (Operational Mode), which terminates all running CableID verification tests. Because CableID verification is performed on a port-pair basis, the test can only be terminated after the current port-pair verification completes and before the test starts for the next port-pair: the in-flight port-pair runs to completion, so the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once the cable-id-status attribute cable-id-state changes to idle; after issuing the command, run 'show cable-id cable-id-status' to confirm the cable-id entity is back in the idle state. 'show cable-id' displays the cable-id entities and takes no parameters.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by the CAD10A and RD20TM cards; the signal is passed transparently in the OPSM. The CableID path starts at the end A port and terminates at the end Z port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. In 'show cable-id-path-<name>', card-type-a and card-type-z take the values RD20TM or CAD10A and identify the CableID capable sled at each end; the value is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at the port-A/port-Z attribute, since when a fiber-connection is created the CableID function checks whether it lands on a port of a CableID capable sled and captures that card type into the CableID path topology. In R8.0.1 the sleds supported are CAD10A and RD20TM. port-a and port-z are port AIDs.

Yes. cable-id-status is the container holding the process status and progress of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you are allowed to issue 'show cable-id cable-id-status' at any time to query the progress. Syntax: 'show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]', Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. cable-id-state is idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running only for the active path), default idle. test-progress is a string 0..255 characters, default 'None': it reads 'Not applicable' if cable-id-state is disabled, or 'N out of M completed' while running, where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number of port-pairs with testing completed.

Each carrier can discover up to one node. It is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. The command 'show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]' shows the local carrier instance that has discovered the neighbor node. local-carrier is a string 0..16; ne-id and ne-name are strings 0..256; ne-type is string 0..64; remote-carrier-id is the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier, string 0..64, and implies a specific remote port id. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use 'show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. degree-number is a uint16 in the range 1..20; it must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. index is a uint32 in the range 1..2, but is always 1 in the 1830 GX since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. port-name is an instance-identifier giving the dwdm-line port of the RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. Use 'show connection-ports*' to view all connection ports in the node, or for example 'show connection-ports-5/1' to see a single one, which returns output such as port-name port-4-1-dwdm-line1.

The custom-tlv command shows the list of Organizational Specific TLV (Type-Length-Value) parameter information. Syntax: 'show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. lldp-port is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string 0..64. direction is ingress or egress. oui is the Organization Unique Identifier of the TLV, the hexadecimal representation of the 24 bit identifier, string 1..6. subtype is the sub-type identifier of the TLV in the scope of the OUI, string 1..507. The value attribute carries the TLV content.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS; although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Before R8.0 a user provisioning one was also expected to set the port attribute external-connectivity to yes. From R8.0, with l0-mode-op set to slte, external fiber connections can represent intra-NE fiber connections between RD20TM ADE ports or between CAD10A DWDM and RD20TM ADE ports. The scope attribute (added in R8.0.1) is general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose; intra-NE connections of that kind must use cable-id, and after upgrade existing entries default to general-purpose and must be deleted and re-added with scope cable-id to enable CableID.

A fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, used in an OADM/ILA topology. It is configured with 'add fiber-connection-<name> [label <value>] [src-port <value>] [dst-port <value>] [fiber-connection-type <value>]', where src-port and dst-port are instance identifiers. An external-fiber-connection is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations; it is identified by string attributes src-node-id, src-card-name, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-card-name, dst-port-name, and carries the scope attribute (general-purpose or cable-id, default general-purpose). Both take fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way, default two-way, and both have name 0..64 and label 0..256.

Yes. icdp is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its global-switch flag, which enables icdp, takes the values true or false with a default of true, so it is on by default. Commands: 'set icdp global-switch <true|false>' and 'show icdp [global-switch]', available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: 'set icdp global-switch true'.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, part of the Inter NE inter-op feature. It provides an API based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a transponder such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40 and a line system such as FLEXILS, using gRPC server/client as the core mechanism. When the INCI service is enabled, the gRPC server is started and bound to the local IP address; when an INCI neighbor instance is configured, gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: the inci-enabled switch takes true or false with a default of false. Use 'set inci [inci-enabled <true|false>]' and 'show inci [inci-enabled]' in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode, for example 'set inci inci-enabled true'.

Compare the configured and discovered names on the inci-neighbor instance. configured-node-name is the user provisioned name of the remote NE (string 0..128) and is used to compare against discovered-node-name, which is the name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE (string 0..128). discovered-node-id is the node ID of the remote node as received from the remote node, string 0..12. Show them with 'show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]'. neighbor-id is the node-ID AID of the provisioned neighbor, neighbor-address is the IP address of the remote NE, oper-state is enabled or disabled, and alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited with default inhibited.

On interface-neighbor, discovery-cycle-time sets the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent: range 30..300 seconds, default 30. discovery-timeout is the time after which discovery is considered as failed, at which point neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout: range 300..1800 seconds, default 300. Both are set with 'set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. discovery-enabled is the switch to enable or disable discovery on the local interface, true or false, default true. neighbor-adjacency-state values are blackout, discovery, holding and unknown, default unknown; oper-state is enabled or disabled, default disabled. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

No. The links container within the topology is dynamically filled in by the system, which allows the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command is simply 'show links' and it takes no parameters; it is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related nct-connection command likewise shows connectivity information between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE, and those links are also dynamically filled in by the system.

The global lldp hold-on-timer is the time to keep neighbor information in the case where the neighbor does not have an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. It is a number of seconds with a default of 900. Configure and view it with 'set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]' and 'show lldp [hold-on-timer]', in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode; for example 'set lldp hold-on-timer 60'. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. On a per-neighbor basis, the lldp-neighbor ttl attribute gives the seconds until the remote system information expires, and if the remote system does not provide a ttl value that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer.

'show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]' shows the LLDP local system information sent on an lldp-port. The 1830 GX NE uses the chassis serial number as chassis-id (chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component), the port AID as port-id (port-id-subtype is local), the port name as port-description, the NE name as system-name, and for system-description the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> build <software label>'. All those strings are 0..255 characters. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities take the values router and bridge. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: 'show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4'.

No, the egress direction is not supported. For lldp-neighbor the direction key in 'show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction>' only takes the value ingress, meaning the direction in which the neighbor was detected. The same restriction applies to lldp-port-statistics, whose direction value is also ingress only. Example commands are 'show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress' and 'show -r lldp-neighbor-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4/ingress'. The lldp-neighbor information is kept indefinitely until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. Access: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

No. All counter values in an lldp-port-statistics entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. The counters do freeze in one case: all statistical counters associated with a particular port on the local LLDP agent become frozen whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled for that port. The command is 'show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]'; direction is ingress only (egress is not supported). Counters default to 0; total-ageout counts the times neighbor information is deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL timer expiration, and last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

Use 'show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]', which shows NCT connectivity information giving the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE; these links are dynamically filled in by the system. src-chassis-state and dst-chassis-state take the values node controller, provisioned and unprovisioned. src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: if the port belongs to a commissioned chassis it is the AID of the port, and if it belongs to an unprovisioned chassis it has the format '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>'. Likewise src-chassis and dst-chassis are the chassis AID when commissioned and the chassis serial number when unprovisioned. All these are strings 0..64. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The sndp command controls the SNDP (Simple Neighbor Discovery Protocol) feature through a single attribute, sndp-enabled, which is the switch to control the sndp feature. It takes the values true or false and defaults to true, so the feature is enabled by default. Commands: 'set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]' and 'show sndp [sndp-enabled]', available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, for example 'show sndp sndp-enabled'. The related per-interface settings live under interface-neighbor, where discovery-cycle-time sets the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent.

On 'add submarine-link-<name>' the mandatory attributes are src-node-id, src-port-name, dst-node-id, dst-port-name and degree-target-tx-power. src-node-id and dst-node-id are the NE names of the source and destination nodes (string 0..256); src-port-name and dst-port-name identify the OTS port (dwdm-line) of the degree at each endpoint (string 0..128); degree-target-tx-power is the target launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber link. fiber-length is the fiber length in km of the associated fiber pair ID, decimal64 in the range 0..25000 km with default 0, and it does not include the length of the branch segments. Optional attributes include label, src/dst-card-name, fiber-connection-type (two-way only for submarine links, default two-way), link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list (0..512), bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition (flat-tx or pfib, default pfib) and allocated-spectrum-list (max 32 start/end frequency pairs).

supporting-fiber-connection shows the list of fiber connections supporting a path. Syntax: 'show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]', available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. name is the name of the entity, String 0..64. fiber-connection-list is an instance-identifier giving the supported fiber connection path. It is the same container surfaced by cable-id-path when the -r flag is used: 'show -r cable-id-path-<name>' displays, for a single port, the results from the port-pair including all cable-id-path parameters plus the supporting fiber connections, for example output lines 'supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6' and 'fiber-connection-list supporting-fiber-connection-R1'.

Use `clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>` (Operational Mode) to manually remove existing topology neighbor information. The target is an instance-identifier and may be: an lldp-neighbor instance, discovered via LLDP; a carrier-neighbor instance, discovered via ICMP; or an lldp-port-statistics instance, containing details associated with an LLDP enabled port. Tip: use `clear topology <tab>` to get the list of valid topology objects. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: `clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1`. To read topology instead, use `show topology`, which is also allowed in Candidate Configuration Mode and accepts inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp.

Use `verify [-f] [type-select=]<value> [[target-select=]<value>] [allow-switching]`. Currently the only type-select value is fiber-connection, e.g. `verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade11`, or `verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true`. target-select is the port instance-identifier of the CableID capable card; if omitted, all paths are verified. allow-switching (values true/false, default false) decides whether CableID may initiate switching on the OPSM: true includes active and inactive paths (system initiated switching), false includes active paths only (no system initiated switching), which is what you use while the system is in service. Precondition: equipment-policies cable-id-control must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, raises CID-verification-in-progress against the NE entity, and is non-blocking; check progress with `show cable-id-status`.

Use the `bert` command in Operational Mode. Start with: `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`. test-id is alphanumeric and is system generated if omitted. 100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31 or PRBS31NONINV, CarrierCTP monitoring uses fec-frames; signal types also include none. Directions are ingress or egress. test-duration ranges from a 10 second minimum up to 1000 hours; the default 0 means an indefinite test. Stop or abort with `bert stop test-id=TestX`; test-id is mandatory for stop. Also available: `bert get` (all, or by test-id, resource or AID) and `bert delete test-id=TestX` or `bert delete resource=card-1-6`. Multiple simultaneous BERTs can run on a facility if each individually meets the pre-conditions.

The cid-ptp facility is system created, not user created: it is created automatically when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A. It represents the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. Its managed-by attribute is system (default), and only user-created facilities can be user deleted, so there is no add or delete for cid-ptp; the supported commands are `set cid-ptp-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>]` and `show cid-ptp-<name> ...`. admin-state is not editable and the only supported value is unlock; CableID operation is not affected by the cid-ptp admin-state. The used attribute is true when CableID functionality is supported (default false). Example: `show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid` or `show cid-ptp-1-6-spu`.

eth-zr is the Digital Coherent 400ZR interface, auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type is 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate is 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable and shown, with values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7; the default is ofec. Degrade monitoring uses two pairs: FEC Detected Degrade with fdd-monitoring (enabled/disabled, default disabled), fdd-threshold default 0.0195 avg BER and fdd-clear-threshold default 0.01062 avg BER; and FEC Excessive Degrade with fed-monitoring (default disabled), fed-threshold default 0.0206 avg BER and fed-clear-threshold default 0.01125 avg BER. All four thresholds are decimal64(9) in the range 0.000000001..0.1 average BER. Example: `set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000`.

The limit is set by the max-packet-length attribute of the ethernet facility: `set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value>`. It is the maximum transfer unit for the ethernet facility in octets, with an 1830 GX G30 range of 1280..18000 octets and an 1830 GX G40 range of 1518..18000 octets. The default is 1518. Two restrictions apply: max-packet-length is configurable on card level only and applies to all interfaces on that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs. The attribute is used in set and show.

Use `show facilities`. It shows the system facilities configured on the node and takes no parameters; access is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. The output is a flat list of facility instance names, for example on an 1830 GX G40 node: super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni, odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1 and odu-1-4-T13. Use the per-facility show commands (for example `show ethernet-<name>`) for the attributes of any listed instance.

The fc facility is managed with `set fc-<name> ...` and `show fc-<name> ...` in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. Fibre Channel specific attributes: fc-type (read-only) with values FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G, FC32G; tts, which enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support for the 32GFC client, values enabled/disabled with default disabled; and laser-toggling-for-tts, which enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled for the 32GFC client, values enabled/disabled with default enabled. Generic settable attributes are label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default, plus BMP, openZR+, FlexE-4x100G, GFP-F, GFP-F-extOPU2, AMP, iGMP, none), loopback (none/facility/terminal, default none), loopback-mode, test-signal-type (default none), test-signal-direction (default ingress) and test-signal-monitoring (default false).

The flexo facility exposes foic-type as a read-only attribute. FOICx.k means using k parallel lanes to carry a FlexO-x interface, where order x is the interface rate in units of 100G, a unique FOICx.k identification per G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR. Supported values are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with foic4.8 the default. fec-type is also read-only: not-applicable, cfec, ofec or noFEC, default ofec. resource-mode is settable and selects the resource mode configuration to support either (ADM) add-drop or (XC) add-drop with regen; values are ADM and XC, default ADM. Example: `set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'`. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds.

Creation requires four mandatory attributes: `add flexo-group-<name> carriers <value> rate <value> modulation-format <value> group-id <value> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [fec-type <value>]`. carriers is the list of carriers bound to this facility, a string of length 1..32. rate is the carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s. modulation-format is one of not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM or BPSK. group-id indicates the interface group instance that the FlexO-x interface is a member of, an integer in the range 1..1048575, and it must be unique in the NE. Optional on add: label (0..256), admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed) and fec-type (not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7; default ofec). Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

high-speed-monitoring has just two attributes, both settable and showable: `set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>]` and `show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]`. enabled is the user configurable switch to enable or disable high speed monitoring, values true or false, default false. port is the user configurable port, a uint16 in the range [1..max], default 57500. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

The interlaken facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface, and is managed with `set interlaken-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [loopback <value>]` plus a matching show, in Operational or Candidate Configuration Mode. Only four attributes are settable: label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed or inhibited; default allowed) and loopback (none, facility or terminal; default none, where facility tests towards the facility side and terminal towards the terminal side). capacity is read-only and is the total capacity for the interlaken interface, 500 Gbit/s, which is also its default. managed-by is system only, so the facility cannot be user created or deleted. Example: `set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1`.

Auto-in-service on a line-ptp is controlled by two attributes, both available on add, set and show: auto-in-service-enabled is the auto-in-service switch for the facility, values true or false, default false; valid-signal-time is the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal used for the auto-in-service mechanism, a number in the range 1..7200 minutes with a default of 480. A read-only companion, remaining-valid-signal-time (range 1..7200 minutes), shows the actual remaining time for the facility to be automatically enabled by the auto-in-service mechanism. Example: `set line-ptp-<name> auto-in-service-enabled true valid-signal-time 480`, and `show line-ptp-1-2-1` displays auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes, remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes. Access is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

They are two different commands. network-xconnect is a read-only overview: `show network-xconnect` takes no parameters and shows the list of services of multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE (Operational or Candidate Configuration mode). nw-xconnect is the per-instance object you actually provision: `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`, `set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>]`, `show nw-xconnect-<name> [AID] [oper-state] [avail-state] [endpoint1] [endpoint2] [xcon-type] [rate]` and `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`. So use nw-xconnect to create, modify, view or delete an individual user channel cross-connection, and network-xconnect to list what is commissioned.

User channel cross-connections are created with `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`. The supported xcon-type values are L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0, L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC, with L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 the default; a direct GCC-to-OSC type is not offered. To bridge an Ethernet management port onto a GCC0 use `add nw-xconnect-test xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 endpoint1 comm-eth-1-12-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-ch1`, having first set `set comm-eth-1-12-ETH4 mode L1`; onto an OSC use `add nw-xconnect-test1 xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-eth-1-16-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-1-6-dwdm-line-OSCX5`. endpoint1 and endpoint2 are mandatory instance-identifiers. rate is 1..20 Mbps, default 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC.

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created; when a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use `show odu` to determine whether the ODU exists.
