What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, the ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G) facilities that XCONs are mapped into, with `add odu-<name> odu-type <value> ...`. The stated pre-condition is that the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added, and each LO-ODU points at its high order parent with parent-odu. The class attribute is set by the system: high-order for the top-most ODUCn/ODUk entity created by the system, low-order (the default) for its children, and mapped for a mapped client signal. Example: `add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80`.

Yes. Each direction has its own values: the odu-diagnostics instance is addressed as `odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>`, where direction is ingress or egress, and add, set, show and delete all take it. So you configure the ingress and egress trace independently, for example `set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI-DAPI-OPER`. Per-direction trace attributes include tti-style (ITU-T-G709, where TTI is split into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes, or proprietary, a single 64 byte string; default ITU-T-G709), tx-tti and expected-tti (hex string with 0x prefix, length 1..130, or printable ASCII 1..64), tx-sapi/expected-sapi and tx-dapi/expected-dapi (1..15 ASCII), tx-operator/expected-operator (1..32 ASCII), plus tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting, tim-act-enabled, monitoring-mode, degrade-interval and degrade-threshold.

Yes, FEC is enabled by default on an OTU. fec-mode, the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client, has values enabled and disabled with a default of enabled, and fec-generation-mode, the configured FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver, likewise defaults to enabled. fec-type defaults to ofec, and the permitted values are not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. All three are available on add, set and show, for example `set otu-<name> fec-mode enabled fec-type ofec`. Access mode is Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting attribute on the otu-diagnostics instance for the direction you care about. It indicates whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, if reported, the criteria on which it is raised. Values are disabled (the default), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER and SAPI-DAPI-OPER. To alarm only on a mismatched source trace, choose SAPI: `set otu-diagnostics-1-1-1-OTUC1/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI` on a G30 node, or `set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI` on a G40 node. This works with tti-style ITU-T-G709 (the default), where the TTI is split into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes; the proprietary style uses a single 64 byte string and the two sets of TTI parameters are mutually exclusive. Whether a maintenance signal is inserted on TIM is controlled separately by tim-act-enabled (default disabled).

The stm facility carries the Synchronous Transport Module N signal, referenced to ITU-T G.691. The read-only stm-type attribute, the type of SDH signal (STM-N), has exactly two values: STM-16 and STM-64. The facility is managed with `set stm-<name> ...` and `show stm-<name> ...` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Settable attributes include label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti, loopback and loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), and the test-signal attributes. Example: `set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP`.

That is the Tributary Disable Action, set with tributary-disable-action on the trib-ptp facility. It indicates what action the network element performs towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, including shutting off the laser or inserting an appropriate replacement signal. Values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais, and send-nos for 1830 GX G30 only. Example: `set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off`. tributary-disable-holdoff-timer gives the hold off time of client shutdown or replacement signal in the egress direction, a uint16 of 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0 meaning holdoff is disabled; it applies only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff. Related switches are near-end-tda (default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true).

Create a Layer 1 digital service with `add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]`; source and destination are instance IDs, direction supports only two-way (also the default), label is 0..256 and circuit-id-suffix 0..48. After creation only label and circuit-id-suffix can be changed with set; use `show xcon-<name>` and `delete xcon-<name>` for the rest. Examples: `add xcon-11 source odu-1-1-3-ODU4 destination odu-1-1-1-ODU4-1` on a G30, `add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1` on a G40. protection-type is read-only and represents the protection type this XCON has, with values y-cable, snc-n, snc-i and unprotected, the default being unprotected. managed-by defaults to user, and only user created XCONs can be user deleted.

An L2-bridge is identified by its bridge-name, a string of length 0..64 used in the instance name, for example `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name>`. Only two attributes are configurable: chassis-name, a leafref giving the associated chassis name for this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. The syntax is `set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>]` and `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]`. Both attributes are used in set and show, and neither has a default. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use the clear app command, which clears third party apps: `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`. The app-name parameter is the third party app name, and the -f flag forces the command without confirmation. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. If you only want to stop an application rather than clear it, set the third-party-app enable attribute to false (`set third-party-app-<app-name> enable false`); when enabled the app is started and is also enabled again upon system restart, when disabled the app is stopped. The state attribute reports running, stopped or failed, with stopped as the default.

Use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]`, available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. app-name is a leafref to an existing third-party-app app-name. command takes one of three values: restart, which restarts the third party application; netls, which shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers; and exec, which executes a third party application operation given in parameters. target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a specific chassis/card AID; it is a string or the keyword system, and defaults to system. parameters carries optional values passed with the command, up to 50 elements, and applies when command is restart or exec.

Yes. Use the call-home command, an Operational Mode RPC that executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server: call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>. It forces a connection attempt, and if the dial-out-server is currently in the 'connecting' state the command forces an immediate attempt instead of waiting some time before retrying. The only parameter is dial-out-server-name, the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default); -h displays help. Pre-condition: the dial-out server must already be configured for the command to execute properly. Examples: call-home collector-x, call-home callhome1. It is also the way to connect a dial-out-server manually when its auto-connect is false.

Use show current-subscription-<subscription-name> [related-session-id] [related-dial-out-server] [session-type] [session-protocol] [encoding] [transfer-mode] [updates-only] [user-access], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. encoding specifies the data encoding scheme for data sent to and from the target device, with permitted values json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf; the default is json-ietf. transfer-mode specifies the data transfer mode: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off) or poll (values sent in response to a poll request); the default is stream. session-protocol is gnmi (default gnmi), and session-type is one of gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel or gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc. updates-only (true/false, default false) sends only changes rather than the initial current value.

No. YANG data models are not all loaded by default: the enabled attribute of data-model defaults to false. Use set data-model-<name> [enabled <value>] to load or unload a model, and show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled] to view them; show data-model with no name lists all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Parameters: name, the model name, String (length 0..256), used in set and show; description, the data model description, String (length 0..256), show only; enabled, true or false, default false, which loads/unloads the data model. A loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces.

A dial-out-server takes retry-policy with values progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop or retry-forever, defaulting to progressive-back-off. retry is the number of retries, Integer 0..5, default 3, and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop. timeout is the time before the next retry, Integer 1..255 seconds, default 10, and is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. port is the dial-out-server session port, Integer 1..65535, default 4334, which is the default for the netconf protocol over ssh. protocol is netconf or restconf (default netconf) and transport is ssh. Configure with add/set dial-out-server-<name> address <value> [protocol] [port] [retry-policy] [retry] [timeout] [auto-connect]; auto-connect defaults to true.

Yes, gNMI/gRPC is enabled by default: the grpc object's enabled attribute defaults to true, and the port that listens for gNMI access via gRPC defaults to 50051. Use set grpc [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity <value>] and show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity], in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. gnmi-get-encoding-granularity controls the granularity of data in JSON-encoded gNMI Get responses: per-path puts all path data in one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Disable with set grpc enabled false.

NETCONF listens on port 830 by default (port-number, uint16, range 1..65535) for NETCONF access via ssh, and hello-timeout defaults to 2 seconds, with range 1..3600 seconds. hello-timeout specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; the session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. Use set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [annotate-cli-name <value>] [static-info-in-notifs <value>] [hello-timeout <value>] and the matching show netconf, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. enabled defaults to true and cannot be set false from within a NETCONF session. annotate-cli-name defaults to false; static-info-in-notifs holds at most 10 YANG identifiers, string length 1..64.

Plain HTTP is available but off by default: http-enabled defaults to false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. https-enabled defaults to true, and the overall enabled switch defaults to true. http-port defaults to 8080 and https-port defaults to 8181, both in range 1..65535. Session lifetime is set by cookie-timeout, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, Number in range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Use set restconf [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [cookie-timeout] and show restconf, which also shows api-root (String length 0..64), the root of the RESTCONF API. Example: set restconf cookie-timeout 10.

Use show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count] in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. snmp-engine-id is the SNMP EngineID of the NE, a read-only String of length 0..256 shown only via show; it follows the EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC address Pool of the NE. engine-boot-count is a show-only Number (uint16), default 0, counting how many times the engine has restarted. Configurable attributes are set with set snmp [enabled <value>] [port <value>]: enabled is true/false with default true for global SNMP access, and port is the port where the NE listens for SNMP requests, Number in range 1..65535, default 161. The trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object.

No. The snmp-community attribute community-string-access, the SNMP access right of the community string, has read-only as its only permitted value and read-only as its default, so a read-write community cannot be created. Use add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. name is the name for the community, distinct from the community string itself, String length 0..64; community-string is the community string, String length 1..32; enabled is true/false with default true. Example: add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true. Note the trap-community-string lives in the snmp-target object.

Add a trap listener with add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. snmp-version is v2c or v3, defaulting to v2c. trap-community-string is the community string used for SNMP traps, String 0...32, with the default infinera. target-port is the UDP port number, Number in range 0..65535, default 162, and target-transport is udp, default udp. target-name is String 0...32; enabled defaults to true; snmpv3-user only applies when snmp-version is v3. Example: add snmp-target-mytarget snmp-version v2c target-ip 10.220.225.10 target-port 162 target-transport udp trap-community-string public enabled true.

A new SNMPv3 user gets user-sec-level no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy protocol priv-protocol offers DES, AES128, AES192 and AES256, with AES128 as the default. auth-protocol has SHA as its only value and default. Create with add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]; auth-passphrase and priv-passphrase are mandatory on add and are Strings of length 8...64, and snmpv3-user-name is String length 1...32. set, show and delete forms exist, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123.

The subscription-path attribute subscription-path-mode controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change or sample, with target-defined as the default. Use show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]. sample-interval is the time in milliseconds between samples of the telemetry data source, default 0 (set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription with no sample-interval set, the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. heartbeat-interval is the maximum interval in milliseconds between updates, default 0; for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset and heartbeat-interval below 10 seconds, the system adjusts heartbeat-interval to 20 seconds. suppress-redundant (true/false, default true) suppresses redundant updates.

Use show subscriptions. It shows a list of subscriptions and takes no parameters. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For a list representation of the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, also known as the current telemetry subscriptions, use show current-subscription-<subscription-name>, which reports related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. The individual paths of a subscription are listed with show subscription-path, or show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> for one path. show telemetry displays the persistent and dynamic telemetry configuration.

Telemetry is configured through the telemetry object, using show telemetry and set telemetry id <string>, in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The command configures persistent and dynamic telemetry, and the telemetry object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. It has a single parameter, id, described as persistent and dynamic telemetry, of type string with length 0..4096 and no default. Example: show telemetry displays the telemetry subscription. The related objects are subscriptions (show subscriptions), current-subscription for configured telemetry subscriptions including encoding and transfer-mode, and subscription-path for per-path mode, sample-interval and heartbeat-interval.

Use show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable], or show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]. The state attribute reports the third party app state as running, stopped or failed, with a default of stopped. No, it is not enabled by default: the enable attribute is true/false with a default of false. enable is the third-party-app enabled state; if enabled the app is started and stays enabled upon system restart, and if disabled the app is stopped. Configure with set third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. version and vendor are string 0..64, product string 0..256, information string 0..1024.

Use add <tab> to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time, and add -h for help. The add command creates a new managed entity in the system database: add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...], in Operational mode or Candidate Configuration. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided upon creation; if a mandatory attribute is not given in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Non-mandatory attributes can also be initialized as attribute-value pairs. -v validates the command only, without creating the target entity, replying OK if valid; -m merges, a best effort add that creates the entity if absent and updates it with the supplied attributes if present; -f forces without confirmation. Entities managed by the system cannot be created with add. The guide lists the creatable entities, from aaa-server through xcon, each cross-referenced to its own command section.

Yes by default. In all cases the clear command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided; -f forces the command without confirmation. -h displays help. clear runs in Operational Mode and clears entries for the specified entity, with each sub command handling a specific type of clear operation. The subcommands are alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology, all of which accept the leading [-f], for example clear [-f] pm ..., clear [-f] system [type=]<value>, clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value>. Note that clear system factory-reset with the shutdown option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes, via set cli show-alarm-columns <value>, which sets the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma, default-columns to show the pre-defined columns, or default-columns,<additional-details> to show that additional column alongside the pre-defined ones. The default is default-columns, and this configuration has a global effect, taking effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3 and set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action. The same cli object carries enabled (true/false, default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port for CLI access via ssh (Number 1..65535, default 22), default-interactive-mode (default true, affecting only newly created sessions) and the show-only script-dir.

Use set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>. cli-lines is the configurable number of rows used for display before pausing the output; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes display. Its range is 10..1000 with a default of 40. The companion cli-columns sets the number of columns for display, range 80..4000, default 80. Show them with show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]; access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, and session-id is a String. Also on the object: interactive-mode (true/false, default true), which is per CLI session and not persistent, and display-timestamp (true/false, default false). Example: set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30.

Yes. The connect command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>], available in Operational Mode. target-address is mandatory and may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address or a hostname if DNS is configured, and it requires connectivity. user-name is a string of 0..64 characters. port is optional; port 22 is used by default, but another port can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Example: connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022, after which the target host is added to the list of known hosts and the remote password is prompted.

Yes, use convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; the CLI command should be enclosed in quotes. target-representation values are netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (the same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted (encrypts a string using security-policies/csp-passphrase), snmp-oids (OIDs for the objects in a 'show' command) and netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing the SNMP request). Multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged where possible, for example two 'set' commands into a single edit-config rpc. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered. Example: convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'.

No. The default command assigns default values to the targeted entities, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes that are only settable at creation. Syntax: default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*], in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; -f forces without confirmation and -h shows help. If attributes are specified only those are set to their default value, otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Examples: default user-peter; default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/EQPTMSMT; default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*; default alarm-severity-entry-*; default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]. Introduced in R9.0, best effort delete bypasses only the check for object existence without returning a failure. Standard behavior, delete <object>, fails if the object does not exist; delete -b <object> does not fail if the object does not exist. The -b option does not raise an error if the specified object is missing, but it may still produce other errors such as precondition failures, and delete -b has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. In scripts you will usually also want -f, which forces the command without confirmation, since delete otherwise displays a confirmation prompt. -v validates only, executing no deletion and replying OK if valid; -h shows help. Deleting an instance removes it and all sub-level objects, and fails if it or its sub-level containers carry services or other traffic affecting configurations.

The exit command logs out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operation mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. Syntax is exit [-h|-f], available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided, which forces the command without confirmation; -h displays help for the command. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as exit -f, so it leaves the mode or ends the session immediately with no confirmation. Example: exit -f.

Use the expect command, which ensures an attribute matches an expected value: expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>, in Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It validates an existing attribute value against an expected value and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes, but wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. It is intended for scripts and automation, commonly to validate system details at the start of a script; if the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode a failed expect stops the script immediately. The -r flag enables regex mode, making the expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123; expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*

Yes, use the export command: `export [<variable>=[<value>]]`. Variables are referenced as ${variable} in any CLI command, which is especially useful in CLI scripts. Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed; they do not survive logout. The variable name can be any alphanumeric string, and the value can be any supported character, including spaces. `export SLOT_NUMBER=2` declares a variable, `export SLOT_NUMBER=` (empty value) deletes it, and plain `export` lists all existing variables, for example `export MYSESSIONID="10.100.152.29:56154"` and `export MYUSERNAME="admin"`. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. `export -h` shows help.

Both launch a Linux bash shell from the CLI, but in different contexts. `shell [-h] [shell command]` launches the shell on the node itself, running as the currently logged-in user with that user's command access; certain commands can be run with elevated privileges by prefixing 'sudo' (permitted binaries include /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient and a set of /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin scripts). Access to shell can be limited to users in the NA, NE, and TT user-groups. `gshell [-h] [<cmd>]` launches the bash shell inside a Guest Container instead, and its pre-condition is that the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both are Operational Mode, both accept a single command to run (`shell ifconfig`, `gshell ls -l`), and both return to the CLI prompt on 'exit'.

No. kill-session closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc.), but the <session-id> you supply must match an existing session-id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>' and cannot match the id of the current session. To log yourself out, use the normal `exit` command instead. Syntax is `kill-session <session-id>`; session-id is a string with no default. Use `show session` first to display the list of current sessions and pick the target id. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: `kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212`.

Use the message command: `message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]`. By default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions, so `message "System will reboot in 5 minutes"` reaches everyone. message-content is a string of 1-4096 characters. The target parameter defaults to 'all' and accepts: all (all CLI sessions), local (only local sessions, serial console or CRAFT), remote (only remote sessions, e.g. SSH), a session-id (only that specific session), or a username (all CLI sessions of that user). Example targeted send: `message "System reboot in 5 minutes" 0.0.0.0:36`. Access mode is Operational mode. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions.

Properties are type-specific, auto-instantiated by the system but user-configurable, addressed as property-<card-name>/<property-name>. Syntax: `show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description]` and `set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]`. Two property-names are supported. fast-client-recovery indicates whether fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures; values are disabled and enabled, default disabled. max-packet-length indicates the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO; range 1518 to 18000, default 1518. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled`.

Use the run command. `run task [[task-name=]<value>]` executes a previously configured/defined/scheduled task, for example `run task collect-diag`; task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name. `run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]` executes a script, where script-name is a relative path to the script directory and arguments are optional. Flags: -q runs the script in quiet mode showing only command output; -r executes it as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the script content; -e sets the error option, continue (default), stop, or rollback. Pre-condition: the task or script to be called must be defined. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: `run script config.cli -e=stop -q`.

Both add/set/show/delete user-configurable scheduled commands and both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode, but task is the richer, fully specified object. `add task-<name> command <value> ...` supports enabled (default true), label, alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), command (string 1..1024), command-type (cli), frequency (string 0..32 in the form '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]', e.g. '5d 12h'), number-of-runs (no-limit or 1..65535, default no-limit), start-time, end-time (default never), persistent (default true), plus read-only task-status (scheduled/disabled/finished/ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output. scheduled-task covers the same idea through `add/set scheduled-task-<name>` and `show scheduled-tasks`, with command 0..1024, frequency w/d/h/m/s (empty means a single-occurrence task), start-time and end-time as YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, persistent default true, and previous-result values 1 or 2; it has no label, alarm-report-control or number-of-runs.

Only SA users can access the list of all sessions; all remaining users can only see their own session. Use `show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]`, or plain `show session` for the list. session-id is the IP address and transport-layer port number of the session, or 'NA' if the session was initiated from the serial port. session-type can be cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui or gnmi; session-protocol can be telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https or http. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI when using Cookie Based Authentication; the session keep-alive defaults to 5 minutes and is changed with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute.

Yes. `set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]` requires at least one attribute-value pair, and multiple pairs are allowed as long as they belong to the same managed entity. Use the wildcard (*) to set an attribute on multiple instances at once: as the whole instance key (card-*), as a single instance key (port-1-4-*; port-1-*-3), as replacement of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), to auto-complete instance keys (user-admin*; ethernet-*), and to auto-complete attribute names (admin* for admin-state). [] gives ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Filters in the form <attribute>=<value> restrict the set to matching entities, e.g. `set port port-type=line admin-state lock`; `set port-1-4* admin-state lock` locks all ports on card-1-4. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances; -f forces without confirmation and -v only validates.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE, and TT user-groups. The shell is launched using the currently logged-in user and only allows commands accessible to that user, so privileges follow the CLI account. Certain commands and scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing them with 'sudo'; the permitted set is /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient, and the scripts /bin/bash /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin/ clear_downloads.sh, config_dns.sh, config_ip.sh, download.sh, install_os.sh, show_dns.sh, show_downloads.sh, show_ip.sh, show_route.sh, tunnelctl.sh, install_app.sh, remove_app.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and docker.sh. Syntax `shell [-h] [shell command]`; access mode is Operational Mode.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request with an <entity-id> instead of a generic <entity-type>, with filters (<attribute>=<value>), or with named attributes. Wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, user-admin*, admin* for admin-state) and [] ranges/lists (card-1-[1..4], interface-[DCN,CRAFT]) also scope the request. Flags that reduce volume include -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) and -o (state/read-only attributes only); -r=<n> limits recursion to n levels, while -r with no value uses full recursion. Piping to `more` displays long output page by page. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use `simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>])`. The trigger values are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru; note that plug-out-fru is not supported. Equipment simulation needs the holder-AID (string 1..64) matching the card slot or tom port, plus the card type; subtype is optional for plug-in, though real hardware always has the subtype well defined. For alarms, alarmed-entity and alarm-type are given, and if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared; alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto, chosen by the system. The command works on a simulator and on a real system, but simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real HW, for example plugging out hardware that is physically present. Access mode is Operational mode. Example: `simulate plug-in-fru 1-5`.

Yes. `sleep <time in seconds>` specifies a delay, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. For 100 milliseconds use `sleep 0.1`; for one second use `sleep 1`. The single parameter is the duration of the delay in seconds, with no default. `sleep -h` displays help for the command. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode, so it can be used inside CLI scripts run with the run script command as well as interactively.

Use the task command with a start-time and no frequency: leaving frequency unconfigured makes it a single-occurrence task. Example from the guide: `add task-db_backup_once command "upload database file-server=xfr1" start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label "DB Backup once"`. This requires that the file server xfr1 be configured before the command is used. name is a string 0..64; command is a string 1..1024 and its content depends on command-type, which is cli; start-time is the timestamp to start the task (for periodic tasks it is the first trigger); end-time defaults to never; enabled defaults to true so the task can be disabled without deleting it; persistent defaults to true so the task survives a system restart; alarm-report-control is allowed or inhibited, default allowed. Check progress with `show task-<name>`: task-status will be scheduled, then ongoing, then finished for a single-occurrence task, with next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success/fail) and previous-output. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

terminate stops a running operation, in Operational Mode, in these forms: `terminate location-led <entity>` ends a location led test previously started by the activate command, targeting a chassis or a particular card (no effect if no test is active); `terminate otdr [entity=]<value>` stops an ongoing OTDR measurement for the given port; `terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>` stops an ongoing OTDR fiber check on an OTS-R entity, aborting the scan abruptly, restoring the otdr ne function attributes and reverting ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state (if that state was fail, the PUMPS-DISABLED-OTDR-TEST-FAILED alarm is raised again), while logs and available OTDR result files are saved; `terminate loopback [entity=]<value>[,<value>]*` terminates WSS loopback on NMC entities, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated (channels cannot be added or removed from an active loopback); and `terminate cable-id` stops a CableID verification test. Confirm the CableID stop with `show cable-id cable-id-status`: the test has stopped once cable-id-state is idle. Because CableID verification runs per port-pair, the current port-pair test completes first, so the maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. Examples: `terminate location-led chassis-1`, `terminate otdr 1-1.3-7`, `terminate otdr-fiber-check ots-r-1-1-dwdm-line`, `terminate loopback nmc-RD66-1-8-ad1-191337500`.

update does not take an arbitrary attribute and value the way set does; it triggers a specific predefined update action on an object, selected by <type>. Syntax: `update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*]`. The four types are span-loss-alarm-threshold (re-evaluates and updates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold), filter-insertion-date-now (updates the chassis's dust filter insertion date to the current date), set-under-commissioning (sets the entity to under commissioning state, applicable to NE entities in SLTE systems) and clear-under-commissioning (sets the entity to Ready for Service state, also for SLTE NE entities). entity-id names the instance(s) to update, and multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). Access mode is Operational mode only, unlike set which also works in Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: `update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line` and `update filter-insertion-date-now chassis`.
